


The Moth, The Mountain, and The Middle-Aged Man: 
self-awareness Communes with Self-Consciousness


Dedication:

These words are dedicated to those of us who are just out of reach. To those of us who find ourselves imprisoned and unable to touch the soil. 

Come, dear reader, be with me now as we taste the grass mingled with our saliva. Let this fluid act as a conduit between us and our Great Mother. Come. Come. It is time.

To Cliff
To Shawn
To Ken
To all those in my life who could see no other path than to take their own,

And to Kyle, who died “over there”


Introduction:

The Moth, The Mountains, and the Middle-Aged-Man is a story of redemption. A story of a Universal man who says “yes” to life over and over again. The story of a fluid man. The story of an individual who lets go of certitude to find a Universal love within himself. The story of a man who makes peace with his feminine nature. It is the story of a son who longs to make peace with his father. The story of a father who longs to be with his children. It is the story of a man who loves his Mother. It is the story of a Universal Snake which unwinds within a man and shoots straight up through his spine. It’s the story of a Universal Cat who shows the way back to the wild. It’s a story about the embracing and the letting go of form to allow the deepening of consciousness in the individual first, and then the collective. It’s a story about going to the places that scare you. It’s a story about going past the point of no return. It’s a story about the wisdom in the mushrooms that turned the rocks into soil. It’s the story of the great Chiefs who hold form. It’s the story of the ones who won’t/can’t be held by those Chiefs and the form they offer. It’s a story about becoming trans-rational and integrating all the forms that were forsaken. It’s a story about a writer, an artist, a musician, and a tree Goddess. It’s a story of the One who simultaneously holds the suffering in one hand and the joy in the other. This is the story of a man who is delivered from exclusive bible-belt-fundamentalism and into the absolute openness of the Universal Christ. It’s a story about the infinite depths of the human being. It’s a story about the infinite expanse of the Cosmos. It’s a story about the breath of God, the name that cannot be spoken. This is a story of a finger which points to the moon. It’s a story about giving the finger to the world. This is a story of two shoe salesmen who arrive in a town where no one wears shoes. This is the story of the infinite as expressed through limited form. This is a story of transcending time and time again through the course of a lifetime. This is the story of letting Go. The story of releasing. Of floating. Of trusting. Of Being. This is the story of experiencing rather than believing. This is our story of growing up. It’s the story of a reformed Buddhist monk who asks a man to do a miracle for himself in the rewriting of his story. This is the story of a man who has lost his family and his job. This is the story of a man who broke all the promises he ever made. This is the story of a man who has no home to call his own.  This is the story of a man who has no righteousness of his own, but accepts the free gift of unconditional positive regard offered to him by a Universal Presence. This is the story of a 21 day real-time healing-journey as documented by the man who is on it. This is the story of a narrator who allows the story to be lived through him. This is the story of an author who chooses to die so that his reader may find her new life. This is the story of a Moth. The story of a Mountain. This is the story of the Middle-Aged-Man.

Simply stated, this is a story of a human being who reaches out for help…And this is how our story begins, with a distress call. It is early one Wednesday morning. Our middle-aged-man has just eaten some psychedelic mushrooms. But this time, instead of allowing himself to sink into the soil, he begins writing. He begins writing an email to two friends, a husband and wife who own a pubishing company. He wants to send them a draft of the autobiography that he has already written, but he doesn’t—he withholds—instead he starts a new story. A story that begins now with the sending of this email to his two new friends—his two new friends who just happen to own a small publishing company, Muse Harbor

Please pardon the draftiness, dear reader, after all, this is a distress call.

Begin draft:

The middle aged man walked the chilled winter streets of a college-cow-town on the Eastern High Plains of New Mexico. The little town was not the type that most people imagine when New Mexico comes to mind. It wasn't anything like Santa Fe or Taos, those quaint cities with mountains for their backdrop where accomplished artists open up shops to sell their creations to tourists. The far East of New Mexico, while still officially a part of the land of enchantment, has much more in common with the rolls and flats of the Texas Panhandle. "The land of the scrub brush and awfully high winds," is how the middle aged man often described it. 

During his first Spring there, seventeen years ago, the sky filled with red dust and the ground bustled with tumbleweeds, some the size of Volkswagen Beetles, which rolled menacingly across Highway 70. The smaller weeds appeared to him as escaping convicts, dashing across the roads, leaping barbed wire fences to continue their manic jailbreak across the fields and over the horizon. As he drove his young family to the nearby neighboring city, he was unsure of what to do when encountering these tumbleweeds. Should he stay his course and collide with them, or slam on his brakes risking a traffic accident and the lives of his children in the back seat? It was often difficult to predict the path and speed of the rolling vegetation. He imagined himself to be Han Solo, navigating the millennium falcon through an asteroid field. (No. He didn't actually imagine himself to be Han. that's the voice that I’m making peace with here. literary voice. fictional voice... this particular young man was still Luke Skywalker...this young man never ever imagined himself as Han, although the fa his dream to fly...he did love the falcon...yes there was something in (every) (this) young man that loved the Falcon very much...but, this young man was Luke. if I can allow myself to comment on my own draft here...is this part of the creative process? is that how this is done? this email as a part of a greater creative effort...consciousness commenting...looking back on itself?).

The truth is...that this young man had never...ever...thought of himself as Han (although, as mentioned before...he did love the Falcon)....LUKE. there was only LUKE. this young man was Luke.

but, back to these weeds...which were real...Luke is trying to manage these tumbleweeds right now...can I acknowledge Han and the falcon in all of this? what about Leia and her distress message? she’s the one who started this whole journey in the first place. Right? More about Leia later.

Ok...really...back to the weeds....the weeds on the Eastern High Plains...yes...it’s capitalized. Eastern High Plains...

He assumed some of the weeds small enough that maybe it would be no-big-deal running over them, but they were still  a problem, as they caught in the grill or the undercarriage and scratched the red paint off his young family’s Dodge Caravan, the same Caravan that would eventually catch fire at exactly mile marker four-twenty-eight on this same highway just a few weeks from now. The red sky, high winds, and sense of isolation on these plains made him feel as if he'd been stationed in a colony on the far side of  mars. (The far side of mars? Mars rotation does not have the same relationship to the earth as the moon, so there’s really not a “far side” of mars. You can’t do the same with Mars that Pink Floyd did with the Dark Side of the Moon. The moon, strange as it has often seemed to me, is always...yes always facing the earth with the same side toward us. And what I’m wondering now is this: Could this anomale somehow stand in support of the flat-earth theory? I mean, the only other planet-like object in the sky that I can see with my naked eye appears to me as a disc, not a sphere. When I first watched a flat-earth documentary I was beside myself in confusion. I kept thinking that at any moment the narrator would reveal the film as some kind of test, measuring the audience’s critical thinking skills. But the narrator did not do that, and that’s okay because it still functions as that test, even without revealing itself as such. What I’m saying is that the documentary really caused me to question myself, “What do you REALLY know about the nature of  our universe that causes you to experience the earth as round? The flat earth documentary is potentially a genius tool in that respect. And it worked that way for me without the narrator having to blow the cover. In fact, maybe it’s more genius that way. Before we knock or ridicule the flat-earthers, maybe we can at least ask ourselves this question. What do I really know that causes me to believe that the earth is round? This type of thinking is going to be important as we move forward in the evolution of this story.)

Seventeen years had passed since that first spring and those dust storms. This slender man with the greying beard had recently purchased an olive-drab jacket from Wal-Mart which he felt he needed for a poorly  timed and insufficiently planned hitchhiking excursion in the dead of winter. Determined to make it  to Oklahoma City to visit his mother, he got only as far as the West Texas town of Amarillo. He arrived there by the generosity of a Truck Driver named Mark...and Joseph....and Brad....

After climbing down from the cab of Mark’s white semi at an Amarillo truck stop , he eventually found what seemed like a suitable on-ramp from which to beg a ride. There he sat, cross-legged with his cardboard sign on the banks of I-40. He remained there for an hour-and-a-half, in the cold, the sun setting. He waited for a ride that was never offered. Frustrated by the law that prevented him from hitching on the interstate, unable to provide his own forward momentum, he resigned to the nearby Denny's and humbly gave up his hitchhike when his younger friend Jerry called to check his well being.

“How are you, my friend? Are you okay? I’m worried about you?”

“Yeah Jerry, I think I’m done. Could you come get me?” said the middle-aged man, the miracle in all that being the man’s seamless transition from determination to surrender without any hint of self-hate (The miracles...that’s our focus here. There are no small miracles. There are no difficult miracles. They are all the same size and difficulty level, flowing from the One heart of love…this is what A Course In Miracles was teaching the middle-aged man)

Some were confused by the hitchhike attempt. His youngest daughter asked,
"Is you car broken, Dad?" 

"No," he answered, "I have just always wanted to put on my pack and start walking. I was answering a Call. Trying to be true to my Self. It was the most honest expression today. It was as genuine as I could allow myself to become."

He had recently resigned his job. But, after handing in his resignation letter he found himself unable to work through his two weeks notice. It was then suggested to him that it might be appropriate for him to be placed, once again, on medical leave. He accepted that offer. With gratefulness he accepted all that was offered.

end draft

Draft:

The middle-aged man wondered, “Will God withdraw his spirit from me?” He paused. A nod to his vipassana practice. “What kind of question is this? Knowing what I know, what kind of question is this?” thought the middle aged man to himself, as he sat on the bathroom floor, his laptop perched on an old milk carton. He closed the bathroom door and ran the hot shower just to heat up the air in the small room. “How wasteful,” thought the middle-aged man. “How can I live with myself?” Samuel Barber’s Adagio for strings played in his headphones. He wondered if this track was too melodramatic for the background to his life’s story. 

(Barber’s Adagio, melodramatic? No, this music comes from the center. This music is drawn from the One Well. This is the music of the death and resurrection. This music bears witness to the BOTH AND... death and life AND that which is beyond the binary. Barber bears witness to all the lives that have ever lived and have been lived through. It is a miracle of perception. It is a miracle which allows us to see into that realm which could not otherwise be seen. It is the gospel that was preached by the Nazarene. It is the Buddha sitting under the tree. It is mother Theresa caring for the poor. It is the surrender in Jihad. It is the Universal Mother who resides in the soil, holding all of humanity. It is Ghandi being influenced by Thoreau. It is MLK holding what he held while he held it, in all the beauty of his imperfect form. It is the peak of the trip. It is the death of ourselves. It is the calm after the storm. Just because it evokes emotion does not make it melodramatic. Allow it to give you your humanity back. Allow it to speak to you what words cannot. Allow it to hold you, to love you, to become you, to be you.)

“This business of writing,” he thought to himself, “It’s really not about writing at all, is it?”

“Father?” said the middle aged man. “
“Yes, Son.” said the middle aged man.
“How will I live with myself?”

This is one of the questions that the middle-aged man asked himself often these days: “How can I live with myself?” This morning he asked this question of the Father who he recognized to reside within his own being.

“Father?” said the middle-aged man. “Yes, Son,” said the middle aged man.
“How can I live with myself, Father?”

Just the night before, the man sat in a booth with his son-in-law at a local mexican restaurant in the college-cow-town. He and the son-in-law were making an exchange. The inner pocket of the man’s olive drab jacket contained a baggie. Inside the baggie was five grams of psychedelic mushrooms. Outside the restaurant, in the son-in-laws car, there was a single tab of LSD. The man and the son-in-law sat together, talking about their most recent trips.

So when the man woke up at 3:30am the following morning he felt guilty. And this is how the man came to ask himself this question. “Will God withdraw his spirit from me?”

“Father?” said the middle-aged man. 
“Yes, Son?” Said the middle-aged man.
“How will I live with myself. My son in law’s parents would not approve. My ex-wife would not approve. Will you withdraw your spirit from me?”

The man’s consciousness hung there as Arvo Part’s Spiegel im Spiegel emanated very softly from his headphones. He sensed somehow that God had not withdrawn his spirit, that this business of living with one’s self had more to do with how willing he was to accept himself in contrast to how willing God was to accept him. 

“It is true,” thought the man, as he sat cross legged on the floor of the steamy bathroom,“writing has so very little to do with writing, and everything to do with how to sit on this bathroom floor. It has everything to do with the question, ‘How can I live with myself,’ and especially the tone with which I ask this question.” The middle aged man was a musician, for him, so much depended on tone.

He wondered what would happen if he acknowledged his Father again. What would happen if he left some space there? He had recently been witnessing  miracles arising from that space.

“Father?”

And then it happened. Life opened up right before him, or rather within him. The miracle of consciousness looking back upon itself without guilt or shame, and all the inner spaciousness that comes with an experience like that.

The space between the call and response. The quiet presence before the loving Father answers the call of the Son. The Adagio for strings had returned on the man’s playlist. With every sentence that he typed he wondered if he would be able to continue in this space, this space between the call and response. 

“Yes, Son?” said the Father.

And then there was the next space. The one created after the Father responds to the Son. A space of great creative potential. And in this space the man saw a fork in the road. He witnessed the binary, the inevitable binary of human existence. “Do I go left or right? Do I take this road or that road?”

He sat cross legged on a blanket that he’d crocheted years ago. It was an odd blanket. Eleven feet wide and three and a half feet long. The man had only learned how to do one stitch, which was taught to him by his wife’s cousin, whom he had fallen in love with after she’d told him how she’d had an orgasm while listening to his music. The man had spent many hours trying to perfect this one dense stitch. He crocheted small blankets for his children and skirts for his daughter’s Barbie dolls. Finally, his stitch was consistent enough that he embarked on the impossible task of a blanket that he imagined would be able to cover his family of five as they sat on the couch, watching TV together in their home. 

But he never finished the blanket. It was never big enough to cover them . And within the memory of the blanket he’d escaped the binary for a brief moment. “Writing has very little to do with the binary,” thought the man. “Well, it has very much to do with the binary, in the sense that the fork in the road will always present itself, and the point is to wait at that juncture until the road-that-is-not-a-road appears.” He wondered how many times he could experience this miracle. “That’s a ridiculous thing to wonder,” thought the man. “Writing,” thought the man, “has very little to do with writing and everything to do with this miracle. This miracle of living with myself.” So, he continued to sit cross legged on the bathroom floor, elevated and supported by the half-finished blanket that would never cover his family, waiting for the next miracle, waiting for the next non-road to appear.

Dave had recently described to him a novel that he was writing that was centered around a musician. So, Dave was a writer writing about playing music. The middle-aged man was a musician writing about writing. And Eileen was the one who had surely blessed them both. She spoke with the voice of a Universal Mother, or Universal Sister, or maybe she just spoke with the Universal power...that’s what the middle-aged man had experienced in her voice, some kind of power that may not necessarily deserve a label. Dave was closer to her and I’m sure he heard a diversity of voices. But whatever voice it was with which she had spoke had brought with it a wave of energy that the man was now riding. Her words had come with power to the man just hours after he’d sent them his psychedelic draft. He began to weep at “I SEE you,” and today he kept close to the letter as if his life depended on it.

This is the Letter from Eileen as was recorded:

Dearest heart,

I SEE you. 

Let us both rest in that for the moment. I SEE you. I see beauty, and truth, and love, and light. I see suffering that wants to fade, and a compassionate heart willing to hospice it, for as long as it takes. I see a dream for a better tomorrow, struggling to find purchase in the frozen soil. I see the rising sun in the East preparing itself to grow stronger, warmer, steadier, and to melt the permafrost in men's heart's so that life can blossom anew. 

I see you as tender seedling, unfurling with radical trust and feeling eager to shoot through the coldness of the soil and stretch yourself openly and irrevocably toward the rising sun. 

I rise with you, my brother. I rise with you. 

And I hear you. I hear the way your soul speaks through the words that flow through you. I bear witness to the nonlinear nature of the new state of consciousness that arises, and the experience of Self lovingly, kindly and compassionately harvesting the hard-won wisdom born of ego; including it while transcending the form-limitations of self-consciousness, in order to transform the entirety of this world to a higher fractal iteration than the one we are presently experiencing.

As they were being seated, the middle-aged man smiled and waved with  genuine friendliness in his heart, but he could not help but detect a disconnect, or was that possibly fear in their eyes? He knew that what he was trying to do was impossible. That’s what the miracle is, the allowing of the impossible. He knew that self-justification was pointless. And, it was just as pointless to assume that he knew what others were thinking or feeling about him. Self criticism would only take him back to the psychiatric unit. He knew that he would have to rely on Dave and Eileen to make sense of this draft; and simultaneously he was sure that it was only him that could make sense of this (and he was, as he was now reading over this draft, making revisions and rediscovering the flow that was innate in the spirit of this evolving narrative). 

He knew that he was not a writer in and of himself, and that anything that was born of this process would be the work of a trinity. A sacred three. So, he trusted. He just kept allowing this miracle to happen. Because, after all, the man knew that he was not a writer, he was a guitar player who had been to a psychiatric unit so that he could receive a prayer from a gay black man. The prayer was one of restoration, that’s all the middle-aged man remembered about the prayer. ”The Lord is restoring you,” the man had said to him. 

And now the middle-aged man had discovered that he was also a pray-er of prayers and a miracle worker. And so, he continued in his search for other miracle workers. And he began finding them. And yesterday morning he’d worked a miracle on his chromebook after eating some psilocybin mushrooms. 

The middle-aged man was not making any assumptions about the miracles, or at least he hoped that he was not. In fact, he searched his heart to discover if he was now. All that he knew for sure was that this wave of energy felt real.  And the words he’d received from Eileen and Dave were life-giving.

Now, working a miracle after eating mushrooms concerned the man, because the man had been diagnosed with the disease of “more.” This disease of “more” was common, especially among people of European descent. Early in the colonization of North America, the native Americans had identified this disease as the Wetiko spirit. It is the disease that takes and takes and takes. It is the disease of the mind and heart that cannot and will not stop taking until everything is taken. So this is why the middle-aged-man was concerned for himself. Could he allow the medicine to be medicine without demanding the “more” that the medicine could not and would not give?

He had turned to the mushrooms in a moment of desperation. However, it seemed to him that it was not a move of desperation. A moment of desperation requires a move inspired from a place of stillness. And that is what had happened. The psychedelic experience had been approaching him for an entire year, ever since he’d visited the psychiatric unit in Roswell. Then he went to another treatment center after that in Rio Rancho. By principal, and in the name of his sobriety, he had resisted and resisted the Spirit which was moving him down this path of psychedelic recovery. But synchronicity after synchronicity had shown him this way over the last year.  

He finally allowed himself to be embraced by the wisdom that had turned the rocks into soil. The fungus. He felt emraced embraced by the medicine that was before man. He said “yes” to the ancient method. He risked it. He was risking it now, not knowing what the outcome of this narrative would be, or how the characters would develop, but he was beginning to see that the driving force of evolution was behind him. He was experiencing a Universe that was for-him. A Universe that was out to help him.

Every experience with the mushrooms he’d had since then had been life affirming. No two journeys with the mushrooms had been the same. The man’s inner wisdom created profoundly unique ceremonies for him each time, ceremonies that would never be repeated. The man had taken a picture of a framed quote hanging on the wall of a cabin where he’d taken one of these healing journeys, “There are all kinds of love in this world, but never the same twice,” F. Scott Fitzgerald. And this is how it had been for him. 

He was drawing from the Source that inspired ALL ceremony, the impetus behind the formation of all ancient religions, the inspiration for pre-historic cave paintings. He was seeing into the eternal, the ancient visions which had become the sacred arts. He had seen the Christ in the death and resurrection of a miller moth. In the Kachina dolls he had acknowledged all the chiefs of this world who had been holding form, however imperfect all these forms and their chiefs may be, and he was able to humble himself before these Chiefs, blessing them, thanking them, even offering himself, once again, to this dance-of-form in which we all participate as we dance behind these masks that we find ourselves putting on and taking off and puttting on again.

During these journeys the man saw many things. The man had seen the snake that had devoured him as a child, the snake that underlies all our being, the snake that molts and brings new life, the snake that is feared by the religious, the snake that was lifted up on the cross, the snake that was in the garden of Eden. 

The medicine helped him to feel the care and attention of the craftsman as planted in the door-frame of his bedroom. He smelled his own human body, making peace with his pungent primate odor, seeing himself as a successful expression of the evolution of all consciousness contained in his own species.  He saw his own face as a thunderhead, understanding that nothing is nearly as solid as we so often believe it to be, and in this vision he understood the suffering that we bring upon ourselves by refusing to flow with the dynamic nature of being (the secret of the thunderhead). He’d stripped naked and laid on the cold damp earth in efforts to express his willingness to experience the G_d of cold and the G_d of warmth. He immersed himself in a cold mountain stream by a highway, in his underwear. He began a dialogue with a Heavenly Father as he trekked up a mountain. He agreed to participate in the creation of a new genre. He agreed to participate in the creation of novel form.

Some of these things he experienced under the direct influence of the mushrooms. Some of these actions he’d done afterwards, inspired by what he’d seen, or heard, or felt during the direct experience.

For four years now he had been attending twelve step meetings in an effort to deal with his Wetiko spirit, his ego, his selfish nature. But, what he’d seen in those meetings was that the people in the AA rooms, even the ones with years and years of sobriety had so often been unable to deal with the core of their issues themselves. They had yet to make peace with their own Wetiko Spirit. They were still wanting and wanting, more and more, they just weren’t drinking anymore. And the man found that this experience was true for himself also. 

He found himself wanting. He had worked the steps. He eventually had an authentic spiritual experience supported by the form of the twelve steps and his dear friends  in those AA rooms. He eventually felt at home there, among his fellow ego-addicts. He had felt that he’d finally found his people. He was honest. He was open. He was willing. But the AA rooms, it appeared, were not big enough to hold him. 

No one and Nothing had ever been big enough to hold him.

For all his life, the middle-aged man had gone from place to place, from person to person, looking for a people, or a woman, or a stand-in-father, or a school, or a philosophy, or a religion, a spiritual practice, or a profession, a band, a song, a genre... But, he had yet to find any form that could hold him. Many times he experienced success in his search. In fact, EVERY TIME he experienced success in his search. He had discovered along the way that, as Ken Wilber says, there are many truths, and they are all true as far as their truth goes, but none of them are the whole truth. 

But this wasn’t about truth as much as it was about the primal need to be held. To be embraced. To be touched. To be immersed in some culture, or tribe, or way of being. And now, at forty five years old, this man, having left his wife and children in search of a way to care for himself, was once again riding a wave, hoping to find again, a way to be.

The middle-aged-man longed to be held. And the middle-aged man was often held. He had been held many times in his life. He had been held. He had been loved. He had been nurtured. He had been gifted. Yet still the desperation came, time after time the desperation came. He was hungry with a desperation that could not be satisfied. Was he suffering from the sins of his fathers? What was this suffering? Was it a generational curse, passed down in his genes when a father fails to love? Did it have to do with epigenetics, trauma finding expression in our genome? 

The middle-aged-man had become the father who had failed to love. He was the husband who hated his wife. He had become the one who had broken all of his promises. He had no righteousness of his own. And, by course of life and answered prayer, he had come to meet the requirements to be a disciple of Christ. He had come to hate himself. He had come to hate his mother and father. He had come to hate his wife. And his love for his children may have been translated into a hate for himself, a jealousy for them of what he could never give himself, and therefore could never truly give to anyone else, including his offspring, the most sacred and deserving people he’d ever known. The sickness had enveloped him as he became sickeningly intimate with this hate in himself time and time again.

And this is how the writer began to find a stride, sitting in the half-lotus position in the small bathroom with the door closed and the steam fading in the bathroom. He got up to turn on the shower again, filling the room with steam.

He gave thanks for the steam. He might have forced himself to feel wasteful and guilty for this pleasure, but he allowed himself this luxury, just for today he accepted it for what it was.

He especially wondered now about Dave, and how he might write about a jazz pianist. He wondered what the musician would look like, and if he had suffered in similar ways to the musician in this story. What would that read like?

As he sat back down on the half crocheted blanket, the man remembered how he’d believed for years that if he could just think all the right thoughts that he could be okay, that he could escape this sense of desperation, this Wetiko Spirit that seemed to possess him, this hunger-to-be-held, this disease of “more,” this insanity that seemed to threaten him at every turn. 

He became a student of Buddhist thought and Vipassana meditation. He sat for up to six hours a day trying to make peace with what was happening in his being, trying to make sense of the nothingness of it all. And he was always successful, until finally he was not successful any more. He was always perfectly rational until he could no longer be Reason could no longer hold him. 

Reason was not big enough to hold him. He’d devoted himself to absolute materialism, journeying to the edge of the observable universe, scraping out the insides of his soul with what appeared to be some kind of cosmic melon-baller, all in an effort to rid himself of whatever remnants of religious superstition that might have still been tormenting him. He’d found that marijuana relieved his symptoms and helped him make peace with the world, and that worked very well right up until the point that it stopped working.

It was nearly five years ago that he had first fashioned a noose. It wasn’t a long enough piece of rope to hang himself, but he tied the noose anyway.  He got the instructions off the internet. This thick piece of rope had been hanging around in his studio for years. He tied the constricting loop knot. He tightened it around his neck. It felt very good. Too good. His mind was quiet with the noose around his neck, which was very frightening to the man. He loosened the noose, tried to shake it off, then he set off for his commute to work. But the tears streamed from his eyes so thickly that he could not see the road to drive. His heaving and his sobbing were so great that he had to pull over on the side of the road. He called his therapist, Penny. She told him to go to the emergency room, so he did. 

As he laid in the ER, his head in his wife’s lap, he broke down, grateful for the help which he knew he was about to receive, but which never came. He didn’t get the help because when they asked him if he had a plan to kill himself, he would not say “yes.” He knew what they wanted to hear, but he was only willing to tell them the story of how he had tied the noose, and that was not enough to get him admitted to the hospital. The man had been willing to go to the ER. He had been willing to surrender his clothes and dawn the blue paper pajamas, but he was not willing to say what he knew he had to say to get admitted to a psychiatric unit. It was after this incident that the man gave himself to the help that the pharmaceutical industry had to offer, a sickening and demoralizing experience with prescription drugs.

He visited his first psychiatrist with his wife by his side. The doctor prescribed medications that made him sleep. So, the man put aluminum foil over the window in his studio, turned the air conditioner on full blast, and went to sleep for nearly two weeks. He had lost his job, just the beginning of the deepest sleep that the man had ever known. The greatest suffering was yet to come. He was in the grips of an inescapable death of his false-self. That which was not authentic, all that was not genuine, was passing away. The snake that had eaten him as a boy was shitting him out for a glorious resurrection. So, this is a story about dying. And, of course, not JUST of dying, but the reincarnation that comes after and with and because of the death. Become the incarnated resurrection. This is what is meant by the acceptance of the Christ into ones’ heart. The Christ is the seed that willingly falls into the soil in order to bring forth the tree. The Christ is the ONE who goes into the unknown without resistance. The Christ is the ONE who dies well. The Christ is the ONE who uses the whole buffalo. The Christ is ALL we can see and ALL we cannot see. You know that now. You know that the Christ is not one who can be contained in any old wine skin. The Christ is not one that can be contained by Christianity. The Christ is not one that can be believed in. The Christ can only be experienced. The Christ can only be known by embracing the sufferings, by lowering the resistance to what-is, and then saying yes to the re-incarnation of being, as we allow that Oneness to arise from Center. Christ is our experience when we stop acting compassionate, and we surrender to Compassion itself. When we die to our best patience-act and we become the Patience. When we allow that to flow from our center which we have failed to manifest by strength of our own ego, while patiently and lovingly allowing the ego (flesh) to be integrated, folded in, folded over, like blueberries in a batter. When we acknowledge those shallow (ego) aspects of our being as being shallow, but we also do not exclude them, because it is only the shallower aspects of our being that are exclusive by nature. This is why religions become exclusive, because they are run by the shallower aspects of our being. We are afraid to lose control of ourselves, so we establish these “safe” places (which include buildings and thought structures etc) in which we dwell. “Safe” in quotation marks. They are only safe as far as we can throw them. Because, as they may provide a somewhat controlled environment, a controlled environment is not necessarily where growth is going to happen. The controlled environment may be a place for a new life to incubate, but not necessarily a place where life can come into its fullness. This is how we do a disservice to those of us who wake up, when we try to insist that they stay in the incubator. Imagine a dozen chicks trying to grow up in an incubator. Ridiculous. Or crushing. Or just very sick. And sad.

But sad is okay. It’s okay to see that. To know that. To have been that. To have done that. To have experienced that. And it’s also okay to wake up to a deeper reality. It’s okay that we are suffering. It’s okay to accept that suffering in others. It’s okay to see suffering in others even when attacked.

The middle-aged man lived with his friend and AA sponsor, Dan G. He’d been there with him for well over a year now. However, the backyard had become less attractive since neither Dan nor the middle-aged man cared much for yard work, especially the high level of attention that the landscaping at this home required.

The middle-aged man had now taken his half-lotus to the head of his bed where he sat propped on two pillows with his chromebook perched upon a A Course In Miracles, Volume One. Having retrieved the book, the middle-aged man settled again with the chromebook in his lap.

Dan and Christy laughed and joked upstairs. They both worked in the public school system and today was their first day of the holiday break. The young man was seventeen years old when he got his first paying gig at the Diamond Ballroom in Oklahoma City. The man watched his ex-wife (the mother of his children) scratch and claw her way through school. She was a workhorse, staying up until 2 and 3AM many nights of the week to finally get her masters and then her doctorate. Her hair started falling out. Literally. It was unlike anything he’d ever witnessed before (an observation that was far from true, because he had also seen this happen in his own mother, as he was a child. A woman rising up from under the waves of oppression that had crashed down on all her sister’s that had come before her. Trying to save her own life while fighting for the survival of her family. Yes. He had seen this before).

The clicking of keys was the sound of her.

She stayed up into the early hours and did her work, surviving on coffee and the meatiness of a brutal work ethic which she’d inherited from her family. The Clarks, her people, were determined, smart, and Christian. Their denomination did not allow for musical instruments. When the young musician had first asked the woman to coffee, she was excited. Freud knew about this. He discovered how common incest was. He knew how common it was that a man sought comfort in his daughter (what is he seeking comfort from? And is it comfort he seeks? Or is it a willful expression of his own patriarchal dominance? Is it willful violence? Or is a subconscious manifestation of the trauma that was born in him? Surely it is unconscious. And then Freud revoked it, because it was too much. It was too much for him. It was too much for his world. It was more than he could bear. It was more than his reader could bear. But then he did something else. He turned it all on the “hysterical” woman (was it Freud who did this? Or was it just the macro-ego of his time made manifest in Freud? Early in their marriage, when their oldest daughter was just one year old, the man and the woman agreed together to sell all their possessions, inspired by the story of the rich young man in the bible who approaches the Christ, saying, “Lord what shall I do?” and the Christ says, “Sell all your shit, son. Give your money to the poor. See what happens.” 

The young couple proceeded to follow this example. One afternoon, they put the daughter in the car seat and drove their white Pontiac to the Sonic in Wynnewood, Oklahoma. There, they bought two large limeades for the parents and one small slushie for the only daughter. The young family drove home with the drinks in their laps. They did not drink them. In the green winter wheat field, they poured the sweet drinks out as an offering to the Lord. They didn’t drink the sweet drinks, you see. They poured them out. As an offering to the Lord.

The fathers were scared (sacred)...terrified of the young couples’ decision to sell and give. The terror turned into anger and manifested itself in the young man’s father. “Are you sick son? Do you have cancer? What the hell are you doing? What the fuck’s going on!?” The fathers’ voice trembled at first and then raised incrementally with each question, each interrogation containing a more demanding violence than the one before. 

It was dark and raining when the son slammed down the receiver on the land line at the farmhouse. Hurt and confused by his father’s violent reaction, he ran outside, into the storm, fell to his knees, clutched the soaked soil and tore the grass and the roots in his hands. His tears mixed with rain and mud. The son did not forsee this attack coming. He did not understand the generational curses with which he currently was fucking with. He was not wise enough. He was not experienced enough (Ahhh Jimi Hendrix…Are You Experienced? This was the experience that was now rising from within).

The young man’s father-in-law offered to send the son to a school of ministry. “The devil is roaming about like a roaring lion, son. He would just love to devour a young family like yours.” His father in law had never spoken of the devil before that he was aware of. Not quite like this at least. In such personal tones. 

“No, thank you, said the young man. I am going to follow the Christ’s calling for my life.”

“Son, we’ll send you to a bible college where they can help get all this in perspective for you. That’s what you need. Son, you’ve got a calling on your life. Let us help you answer that call. The devil. He’s gonna chew you guys up. He’s gonna spit you out on the floor. He’s gonna fuck what’s left of the remnants with his steaming cock, son! Do you know what that’s going to feel like, son. Come to your senses, boy. You are going to fucking die! And your family is going to pay the price for this silly little fucking game you are playing. Son. Come to your senses.” 

The mother-in-law was the only one who had a real blessing for them. She was silently happy for their decision. The middle-aged-man remembered this. And she spoke of love and life. She prayed that God’s will would be done. She gave them this gift. It was all she could afford. It was the gift she had been dying to give. He was the son-in-law that she loved. He knew that she loved him. And he was as grateful as he could be.

The young man’s own mother was mostly silent and confused. She was, no doubt worried, as she was surely worried for the middle-aged man now as he continued to struggle. The middle-aged-man, the budding writer who sat at Ron and Joann’s recounting these stories. The one who tells stories, yet attempts to remain rooted in the NOW and the HERE.

Throughout the course of the evening, Ron and Joann held space for these stories as they came to  the middle-aged man. After delivering his good news and reading the email from the publishers, he began to allow some of his hurt surrounding his relationship with his ex-wife to come up (as was his intentional practice to reconcile himself to his pain in community). 

He could feel the hurt right there in his chest, not overwhelming, but not at all comfortable. He allowed the tenderness to surface there, like a buoy on the sea of his being, as Ron and Joann held that space in their sacred home.

After describing his grief to Joann and Ron, and while still holding this discomfort in his chest the middle-aged man described what it was like recently, to be held by the Father in the midst of the great loss, to be held by the Universe, to be held by the One, the Source, Spirit, Love. He described how he had felt so alone and disconnected evn before he had left his wife and family nearly twenty one months ago. In fact, it was this sense of isolation that spurred the great Walking-Away. 

As he sat in the gliding rocker, in the presence of his two friends, he described what it was like to be married to a woman who could not hold him. What it was like to be unable to hold and comfort a woman who was averse to Man. What it was like when he was told, by his ex-wife, to get to work or get the hell out. What it was like when he had suggested a separation during a counseling session and how she had exploded, called him names, and vowed never to return to couples counseling again. What it was like when she had told him that if he ever called her “controlling” again that she would divorce him. What it was like to become weaker and weaker as she got stronger and stronger. What it was like to have a penis in a relationship where penises were only dirty-phallus. What it was like to want to kiss a woman, but not that woman who hated to kiss. Oh! the hardness of her lips! What it was like to make love perpinducularly so that the woman did not have to look into the man’s eyes. What it was like to perform unrequited oral sex dozens and dozens of times because that was safer than sex for her. What it was like to tire of the passionless “other.” What it was like to watch a woman try to climax as if it was a chore. What it was like to withdraw from her intimately, understanding that she did not EVER need or EVER want sex, or kissing, or to be looked in the eyes. What it was like to come back to her for the intimacy that his body and soul so desperately needed but could never ever receive. And finally, what it was like to go a year without sex while she was trying to process through her sexual abuse.

Ron and Joann were good friends. There truly was a dialogue between the three of them that night, but it was not recorded in any way in the writers being (not that he could detect now at least). That night at Joann and Ron’s house was a night that the middle-aged-man released some of his trauma. He had learned over the years how to release a little bit at a time as casually as he could, a lot like Andy Dufresne in the movie Shawshank Redemption.

Andy Dufresne, a wrongfully interned prisoner, is tunneling out of his cell with a little rock hammer—a rock hammer so skillfully smuggled in by his friend, Red. Every day, Andy chips away at the wall in his cell, and every day he releases the debris into the prison yard. Every day, he drops a litle bit of rock and dust right down through his pants. 

And that’s exactly how the middle-aged man had learned to do it to. He’d been chipping away at his trauma for his whole adult life. He’d learned that his trauma was way too much for any one person or situation, so he tried to release it a little bit at a time. He had learned to spread it out over a field of willing and trusted friends, like spreading manure over a pasture, or like Andy in the prison yard, one handful at a time, droppin right down his pant leg, the dust mixed in with the sweat and hairs on his leg.

Ever since he’d had his first conscious Presence experience, the Presence experience which was held by the form that was available. The young man embraced the Presence of G_d within the confines of the form that was available (the form of Christian fundamentalism). And this is the way of things as he understood them even now. He was embraced there in the form of his friend’s home. These two loving souls who were to receive this grateful man on that day. This healing man. This man who was determined to see. This man who wanted his children to live. No. Not just live. This man wanted his children to live a Life Abundant.

The young man and the woman had known that there was a problem, obviously. But they trusted that Jesus had taken care of it. The woman’s only sexual experience up to that point had been with another woman. That is why the young man and  woman had met at church. The woman had repented of her “sinful” behavior and taken refuge in the closest thing to her old religion that she could stomach. She writhed and twisted during the worship services (the serpent rising from within?), the remnants of her trauma trying to surface. 

The young man had his own issues. He had recently been abandoned by his latest girlfriend, the one who was the buffer between him and his own random attraction to other males. He was unable to make peace with his own fluidity. He was scared (sacred) to death that his worst nightmare was coming true—or rather he was living his father’s worst nightmare.

He had a recurring dream. In the dream, he awoke, crawled out of bed, made his way to the bathroom mirror, and saw in his reflection a sleestack. Yes, a sleestack. A green humanoid lizard from the Saturday morning television drama of his childhood, The Land of the Lost. The meaning of the dream, or so he thought, was never difficult to see. He was a monster, the monster that his father was sure to warn him against. He was becoming the monster that could not be held—the monster that could not be known. The monster that would not be seen.

And it was in this way that the young couple emerged from their own deaths It was in this way that their consciousness continued its evolution. It was in this way that the fundamentalist religious form of the American bible belt offered them refuge. This is the form in which the couple incubated. He had no context in which to understand himself that was deeper than the binary. And so it was within the confines of a binary fundamentalism that he found himself making peace with the authentic Life that was arising from within his own being.  

It was within the confines of this form that the couple tried to fit in. This is where they did the most natural thing in the world for a couple their age to do when they feel safe and warm and supported, they started a family. And it was good. It was the most love that either of them had ever experienced in their lives. And this form would continue to appear good for many years to come. 4;30 AM

And so the writer found himself standing there in the great kitchen, facing North. His heels were hurting. “Where were we?” he questioned himself. “We were at Ron and Joann’s. That’s where we were.” He answered himself. 

“Yes. Ron and Joann’s,” the writer remembered now. 

The middle-aged man was held in the embrace of his friends love. He was held in the embrace of their home, that most sacred of forms as it was endowed by their beautiful Spirits. His friends, Ron and Joann held space for all of this to arise. They allowed the man to be. They had witnessed his journey for many years now. He had cried many times in their living room. Just as he had done many times before, he made peace with the refuge that was offered to him on that night. He accepted it just for what it was. Nothing less. Nothing more.

And it was in this way that the writer left Ron and Joann’s home that night. He returned to his own form, the gift that he had been given, these very words that we are sharing in right now, dear reader. These words around which we huddle as we seek refuge from the storms that rage within our own beings.

The writer’s thoracic back ached. He had not moved from behind the chromebook for a timeless moment. He watched all these writings happening before his eyes. He was not required to believe anything that he’d said. He was not required to start a new religion. He simply watched this miracle as the Christ was born again into this world through him. 

He wondered how he would feel right now if somehow this stream of consciousness were suddenly erased from existence. He wondered if another Naked Monk would ask him to do the impossible again. 

There are resolutions aren’t there, my Pema? (The man now confided with his great teacher Pema Chodron). Sentences do have periods, don’t they, my Pema. Paragraphs end, as do chapters in books and in lives. And books. Books have final pages, do they not, my wise Pema? 

“There are also bookends, good for holding us up when we there’s no shelf that will hold us,” his dear Pema responded with a smile. She continued. “Lives end. Entire species sometimes go extinct or evolve themselves to a new form, and therein lies the end of an era. The Universal lungs expand and contract, signaling the end of a cycle. There is also this cycle: The birth. The crucifixion (and the upside down cross, turning form on its head). The resurrection. The life cycle.” 

“Yes, Pema. I see,” said the middle-aged-man responded respectfully to his great teacher, The Universal Pema.

And it was in this way that the man found himself in dialogue with the Universal Wisdom. That which manifests itself in the echoing voices of our teachers. That voice that echoes from our teachers until their words are transcneded and integrated in to the ONE WISDOM that is in us all—That in us which only needs to be reminded of the truth that is already resounding in our bones.

Eli the cat crunched the food in his bowl which sat by the Universal water dispenser. Eli lapped the water from his red Universal water bowl. The Universal heater hummed as it warmed the home in which the Universal man found shelter. He lived by the kindness of his friend and AA sponsor, Dan G. This Universal man was on medical leave from his job. He currently had no income. He had just enough money to pay the next child support payment. 

The writer stood at the island in the kitchen of the great adobe house. He was facing West. He stepped away from the chromebook for a moment. He paused, leaning against the marble countertop. “It is my intention to give way where way is to be given,” he said. “It is my intention to let go, and let Life do the living.”


He did not have enough money to pay child support and also visit his mother for Christmas with his children, as planned. When his mother had asked him what he wanted for Christmas, he paused for several days before answering. “I just want to see you. Maybe some gas money so that I can come see you with the kids.” The middle-aged man had never known this way of life before. At least not in exactly this way. Not by himself.

He observed the barrier between himself and his audience. He remembered (was reminded) that in order for the reader to have her birth, he must disappear. It was his job to disappear, but he was not disappearing, in fact he was just then rising to the surface, nearly encountering the present tense. He toyed with this. 

He imagined it a smart and powerful literary feat that he’d accomplished. He knew that, although he was unaware of where and when this had been done, that it had already been approached, because the world is that big and time is that deep and this miracle of symbolic language was happening long before he was even conscious of these possibilities. Eileen’s words, “new genre” were causing their own little ego death, as they bounced around up there in his head. He then realized that that was part of their purpose.

The middle-aged man had been married to an English professor for nearly twenty years...maybe it was more than twenty years. Is it strange that he is now unable to recall? It seems like something that he should know. Anyway, because he had been married to an English Professor for many years, he was very familiar with that which he did not know. Or rather, he was vaguely aware of how muhch there was out there to be known.

He’d been to many English Department parties and befriended many incredibly gifted and talented thinker and writers, all philosophers of the English language. So, yes, the middl-aged-man had become well acquainted with that which he did not know. It was all out there, a beautiful mystery, and it was this mystery that he was now embracing with all the tutoring from the mother of his children and all those other professors from his past.

The middle-aged man was learning how to write, or rather he was being taught still by the mother of his children, the English teacher. There was a very physical aspect of writing that he found himself working with. Praise be to the laptop and its mobile nature. He was finding different places in the house to write. He now stood at the island in the kitchen, his chromebook propped with the two larger volumes of ACIM (A Course In Miracles).

Because of his wife, he was able to attended parties with people like Ed, the Marxist (whatever “Marxist” means), who had told him about the reified thunderhead (Ed the Mexican-American who could not help but joyfully make reference to reified-beans, assumedly our neighbors to the South). 

All this to say that he knew how terribly smart people could become, and he was quite familiar with his own intellectual limitations. He was just smart enough to really appreciate how smart someone else could be. He could watch it. He could observe it, just like some people watched him play music. However, some of the people he’d met, Like Ed, could play and philosophize, swimming in two realms, creating in that common space. Is this what was happening, was he becoming a Marxist?! Oh God, what would the writer’s mother think if he became a Marxist! “Have I caught the Marxist flu?” wondered the writer. 

And this is how the middle-aged-man worked in and around his beautiful ego which was playfully swimming around in his own being that morning.

Let it be known that he brought forth his message with grace and dignity. 

Let it be known that science is a western Yoga.  Let it be practiced. Let it be informed by Spirit. Let it inform the forms in which Spirit is practiced. Let it be known. 

The rational mind is not left behind as we transcend it. The age of reason, dear reader, was not a mistake. The scientific method is to be felt, and known and experienced. Let it be known that the practitioners of this yogic form are holy men, even if they themselves do not acknowledge that. It is another form of storytelling based in all matter which is all holy and compassionate and holds the story of unity within its very fabric. Matter is not separate from Spirit. All matter is the Christ. All is one. Praise be to all infinite matter!

The Dying God
 
The old man waited patiently in the jungle clearing. White robes,  flowing beard—a dying God—waiting for the man who had much to do with his imminent demise. Sounds of struggle emanated from the jungle brush just beyond the perimeter of the clearing. Using his staff, the old man lowered himself onto a large fallen tree. The disturbance in the underbrush grew nearer. 

Finally, a figure arose from the multitude of wide leaves. And there she stood, just having emerged from the bush. Se was a troubled woman in her mid-thirties—victorian skirts, disheveled hair wilted from humidity, face stained by dirt. She panted from her exertion. She stood there for a moment, relieved to be free from the forest from which she’d just emerged. Then, she scanned the clearing; her eyes met the old man’s. 

“My Lord?” she said, as she stumbled to stand before him.

“Yes, daughter,” He said.

She crumbled at his feet. Her eyes were now fixed on the patterns in her skirt. Tears began as silent, intermittent convulsions in her torso. Then, deep sobs arose from her chest. Her face contorted.  Her eyes rose again to meet the old man’s gaze. Her mouth cracked open in tight expression of grief and thin strands of saliva stretched between her upper and lower lips. She remained there for quite some time. Her breathing steadied as her eyes met His. 

She raised herself slowly to her knees. Then she allowed her torso to collapse into the old man’s lap, hugging his abdomen. His hands naturally came to her head in an effort to comfort.
The two remained like this for a long moment as birds chattered and screeched in trees overhead.
 
“Emma?” said the old man, “Where is Charles?”

“He would not come,” she said. “His stomach is troubling him, and he is filled with anxiety at the thought of seeing you.”

“That is understandable,” said the dying God. “Emma, sit with me.”

Emma lifted herself from the old man’s lap and sat beside him now. She slumped, but she supported herself.

“All Gods must die Emma. It is how it has always been, and how it will always be. You know this to be true. I am merely the projection of what cannot be held in one form. I am only one projection of G_d, one image who points to that which as ALL.”

Emma noticed that a small group of chimpanzees had gathered around them. An adolescent chimp approached the old man and jumped up in his lap. The old man looked thoughtfully into the primate’s eyes. The young chimp’s mother sat down in front of Emma, offering her curled hand. Emma could somehow sense the motherliness in this creature that seemed so horrifyingly familiar in form to herself—hands, eyes, feet, and breasts.

“I am the God of metaphor, Emma, the God of story. Just as all life has changed over time, so do our Stories. This form that you see now, this form that you practice, this lense through which you see life, must pass away to make room for a less…how should I say? A less fatherly figure? Less fatherly, Emma, but not to exclude the Father. The mother is rising Emma. The mother needs to be known if your species is to continue on its path of transmutation. I know that it is difficult for you to understand. I see that you are dying a death. I know that you are hurting. I see you, child. I see you. Let us rest there for a moment. Will you rest there for a moment with me? I see you Emma….Rest with me here for a moment. Let me hold you…

There is a long pause (a menopause)...Emma cries….Emma sobs...She begs for this to be taken from her...She knows this is more than she can hold...She is held by the spirit of this being that is passing into new form.
 
Being speaks…. “This death that you are dying is still the way of the cross, Emma. It is still the way that you have been shown. But, the way that you see me is changing. Your very perception of who I am is transmuting, if you will. This image is evolving, just as all forms have evolved before me. Novel forms are created from this process. You, my daughter are a novel form. You, my daughter, are being born again. Your species is being born again every moment. Without an understanding of this evolution, humanity cannot transcend the binary. Without this understanding the human species is trapped in the delusion of good and evil, trapped in a static prison. 
 
This evolutionary understanding is a result of the birth of the age of reason. Spiral dynamics. The serpent which spirals toward the infinite center of the sun and is drawn infinitely deeper and deeper into this consciousness. Your species is not static. Life is not static. Life is like a thundercloud changing, and ever changing. Without this understanding it is very difficult to experience the One-ness of all life. 

Your husband has discovered a key to unlocking the door to a much broader room, a more expansive field of consciousness. There will be those who take this message and turn it in to something that is not. There will be those who will say that Charles is a heretic. He will be mocked and hated by some for many many years to come, but this is the promise being fulfilled for those who choose to embrace the deepest callings. This is the very heresy that brings your species into a deeper communion with who I really AM. Just as Christ was a heretic, so are the ones who carry the light after him.

It is no different with you, Emma. You are carrying this. You have said yes to your husband and you have said yes to life. He has carried this as far as it will go. It is coming Emma. There is no stopping it. If it is not Charles, it will be someone else. The message of the prophet must amplify the One-ness in the ears of the people. The message of the true prophet recognizes all as ONE and the one as part of the ALL.

The middle-aged man stood, once again, in the great kitchen. The son had set on the world outside. Three lights burned brightly over marble island.
