“There needs, to be a commitment here, my brother. We have to swear an oath of loyalty to one another. We are family, and nothing runs deeper than that. You don’t understand how powerful this could be. We need to make this commitment to one another, that we will never betray one another.”

The younger brother’s plea went on and on. The writer tried to explain that he was not interested in taking any oaths of loyalty.

“Kyle,” he said, “I’ve broken every promise that I’ve ever made in my life. Why would I make a promise to you that when I don’t know that I can keep it. All I can say for certain is that I am here with you, now. I’m having this conversation with you because I care about you. I hope I can be here for you in the future as Life permits. But, I’m not ready to take any blood oaths. That is not something that I am prepared to do.”

The younger brother was having a hard time letting it go. There was more convincing. There was more loud talk, talk that made the middle-aged-man feel like he did when he was speaking with his dad. 

“Okay, bud. I’ve got to go now. Let’s talk on Christmas day. How about that? Would you like to talk on Christmas day?”

The thick piece of watercolor paper where the blue snake lived had begun to serve as a to-do list for his writing project. The dying author ventured out for a walk with the sunrise. He crunched through the golden, frozen grass in his brown, leather, slip-on loafers. He walked on the smooth dirt path through the arching evergreens, where the hard, blue seeds were scattered. He kicked off his loafers. He reached up with outstretched arms, grasping a sturdy tree branch in either hand.
 
The middle-aged-man stood there in the crucifixion position, supported by the trees, acknowledging how Christ had been supported by a tree as he experienced his final ego-dissolution process “It would take the strength of the tree Goddess to support something like that,” said the man to himself. 

The Christ man with the feminine nature in him, supported by the strong form of the tree. The dying author was not trying to create any kind of doctrine in this moment, merely experiencing the meaning of it all as it appeared to him (Praise be to fluidity and the passing stories that come and go with the evolution of consciousness!). He released the evergreens  from his grasp, slipped his shoes back on, and continued down the path where he came to a fork, a binary, a crossroads. 

And so, he stopped.

He stood right there in that place where he could either go left or right. He waited. This fork was the physical manifestation of what he’d been writing about. It had unexpectedly come to greet him on his morning walk with the sunrise (Praise be to the binary fork that offers us the non-path). He waited. Acknowledging. Accepting. Experiencing the moment for exactly what it had to offer. He sensed into his body and all that was. He allowed his thoughts to pass before him, nodding to his vipassana practice. Just as the writer now did now in the typing of the words (Praise be to the words which point to the slivered moon!).

At this crossroads, as he gave space for the creative miracle to arise from within, he sensed again a powerful presence of the feminine within him. He allowed his legs to become a slightly twisted trunk. His hands to became slender branches, reaching up into the sky, caressing the blueness and the morning cold.

He then embodied the spirit of one who was once called “witch.” those pagan women who went to the forest to walk barefoot and experience nature without any barrier, walking in the brown grass and the green alike. He felt her. He felt her making love to this moment. He took off his shoes and held them in one hand as he began walking barefoot, slowly, through the thick, golden, winter grass. His legs crossed over midline as he slowly placed one in front of the other, which resulted in him being more fully aware of his hips and the diminished space between his legs. 

“Whether I look like a woman from the outside or not, right now. I certainly feel like one,” thought the middle aged man. The man tried to let the mental  image of “woman” go. He allowed  the energy of that mental  image of “woman” to pass through. 

Now he was empowered to simply feel  his body, just the physical senses. He walked with this fairy of the forest until his feet got very cold. He quickly slid his shoes on and continued his walk with the sunrise. As he faced East, the sky was deep orange. He made his way through the South gate toward the front of the house. 

The moon was just a sliver in the sky. He greeted the moon “Thank you for your presence, dear moon,” said the Goddess. She greeted the sun into the world. Praise be to the LSD and please God, bless the hands that prepared it.” And so it was that the Goddess gave thanks for the medicine and and for the new day into which She had bee born.

Praise be to the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. Praise be to the snake who circles back and circles back again. Praise be to the man with a lovely feminine heart!

Inside Stone

          “The child who broke
The one who woke up crying
A lovely journey…”
—Book of the Ageless Ophidian, Chapter 9 v15
    translated by Chogyam Trin Pan            

In the thick air of a cool basement, two boys faced one another. They unzipped, engaging each other in a playful sword fight of sorts. The sun’s rays angled in through a half hazed window. 
“We need to get some girls down here,” says the taller of the two. 
A disturbance causes the smaller boy to turn quickly and face the slowly arcing dust motes traveling through the white light. The sound of the opening door from the top of the stairs jump-starts the two boy’s already elevated heart rates. Stairs creaking under feet, the small boy’s grandma chides sharply, “I know what you two are doing down there, and if you don’t stop right now I’m going to tell your fathers!”
The old woman stops half way down the closed stairwell. She stares at the boys who have just barely escaped being caught with their pants down. Trying to look innocent, not knowing now what to do with his hands, the small boy averts his eyes from his grandmother’s silhouette, now analyzing the cobwebs in the corner. The oldest boy stands awkwardly wide-eyed, breathing heavily through his open mouth, staring at the woman’s feet. 
Only now, under her gaze, does the little boy grasp the gravity of his innocent play. He only knows that he does not want his dad to know. The tight faced woman with the tautly wound beauty-shop curls forces the long silence into eternity as her eyes move from one boy to the other—the boys, defenseless against those pursed-lips.

Later, the younger boy found himself. In his grandfather’s quarter acre lot, he weaved his way through stacks of railroad ties, fence sections, camper tops, and rusting livestock trailers. His curiosity renewed—the sunshine and smell of sheep shit freeing him from the pressing weight of the concrete cellar and his grandmother’s threats. He made his way to the red fence at the back of the lot—the calling of birds and the singing cicadas now the only voices in his head. He unlatched the chain on the large swinging gate, climbed the rocky embankment to the tracks, and followed the rails to the wooden Santa Fe bridge.
He chose three grey rocks from the rail bed, as many as his seven year old hands could carry, and ventured out on to the wooden planks. The creek below came in to view through the gaps under his feet. He reassured himself that the space between the ties was narrow enough that he could catch himself if he were to lose his footing. As he approached the bridges’ center, directly over the rainbowed surface of an oily stagnating pool of water, he straddled one of the gaps and dropped a stone. In simple silence it fell for what may have been a second or perhaps much longer, a trick of time the boy held too tightly. He wished his hands were big enough to carry a thousand stones.
The rock broke the filmy surface of the pool…

He was sorry he had killed the baby bird. It hadn’t gone as expected. He had killed adult birds with his BB gun before, their glistening black and purple feathers ruffling as their neck and legs collapsed under the weight of their own body. That made him feel strong and respected, like a hunter. But the bare baby bird was different. He knew, from watching TV,  that it was his duty to put that little creature out of its misery. It was suffering. In fact, he relished the responsibility. The idea of it made him feel so grown up and wise, so responsible. “It is the right thing to do,” he said, relishing the serious and morbid nature of his task. That tiny naked creature, fallen from her nest, screeched and squirmed under the pressure of the curved x-acto blade on its neck. Half way through the surprisingly sinewy flesh, perplexed and horrified, the boy felt the warm red blood on his hands, but the baby would not die. The boy panicked. He stood facing the bird on the altar for a moment, dirt and leaves on his knees. Without the heart to complete the ceremony, he ran, leaving the pitiful writhing life form still squirming on the brick altar. He pushed open the screen door on the back porch, ran inside the two story brick house, and clamored quickly up the stairs to his mother’s room. She was folding laundry. He cried in her arms. The boy was loved for his sensitivity.

From his perch on the bridge, the boy dropped the second rock. Another moment of silence. He could hear his breath hovering over the chasm between himself and the water below. It was that space that held his attention, that quiet moment between release and splash down…
He had once imagined a stone so smooth that it couldn’t be held. Actually, he hadn’t as much imagined the smooth stone, as much as it had appeared in his being. The perfect creamy surface of this stone always contracted into a shadowy, craggling, painful object. Too terrible to touch. Sometimes, if he kept his eyes closed, he could witness this transformation over and over again; the hypnotizing change was out of his control. The little boy could not understand the aliveness of the stone in his vision, or why he was unable to control its transformation.
 He released the third rock. It strayed from its intended course and glanced off the sticky, tarred surface of the tie. The boy lost sight of it and carelessly repositioned his feet so that, with his eyes, he could follow the descent of the falling stone. Losing his footing with the wind, he connected himself to the silence again for a brief moment. He could hear the stone dancing on the rocks below as he regained his balance. His heart came into his his chest with loud thumps that he could feel in his ears. 

That night the boy lay in bed knowing that he could not go to school the next day. This knowing was manifested in a physical sensation that he would one day call dread; it was uncontrollable, like the smooth stone’s transformation into something untouchable. 
If he could make himself vomit his parents would have to let him stay home. He walked to the bathroom and shoved a finger down his throat but was unable to produce any substance from his stomach. He gagged as loud as he could and then plopped down heavily onto the cold white tile by the toilet, hoping his parents would hear his distress, angered by his general state of physical well-being. As he published his post, his phone rang. It was Dan. The man wept with gratefulness as he put the phone to his ear. He allowed his true state to be felt and heard in the presence of his trusted friend.

“Hey, Dan,” the man said, tears audible in his voice.

“Hey, bud, me and Christy wanted to invite you over for a Christmas Eve get-together.”

The man accepted the invitation. He gathered the left over sparkling cider and root beer from the lovely lunch that he’d had with his children earlier that day. He also grabbed a loaf of hard crusted bread. Dan, texted from the driveway, “I’m here.”

The man walked outside wearing his olive jacket and carrying his humble offerings. He was embraced in the loving arms of what-is that night. He was held by the Great Mother. He was supported in the fabric. He found himself in community. The man was loved, and the man had experienced that Love many, many ways. 

But love never comes the same way twice. We find our love today in novel ways. Love comes to us unexpected. And if we are offended and disturbed by that which is unexpected then we may miss our love. Great Mother, open our hearts up for the novel expression of Love in our lives today.

The friends broke bread. The friends drank cold sweet drinks and warm tea. The woman of the house prepared a dip for the broken bread. The piano was played. The guitar was strummed. Voices were raised in song. Gifts were given—and there was even one for the middle-aged-man! 

The man did not stay too long. He did not stay too short. He stayed until he was ready to go, then Dan took him back home.

The man was watching the miracle of Christ child being born in his life. He was giving birth to the Christ daughter. He participated in the forms that presented themselves to him. He was saying “yes” to life. The man was coming to know himself as the very Life that he longed for. He was held. And, there was so much more holding to come, dear reader! So much more awakening to witness. So much more Universal being for us to discover together, dear reader. Come! Come! As Christmas morning awaits! 

Come! Come! Whoever you are. Wanderer, Worshipper, lover-of-leaving.

There is an upward spiral which circles back on itself as our consciousness moves from one stage to the next. I first learned about Spiral dynamics through Ken Wilbur as I was studying his Integrated Life Practice.

Spiral dynamics is the upward spiraling path by which we circle back on our own expereince, and then eventually, as we transcend the rational mind, we integrate all of our life experiences into our current experience. Spiral dynamics is the way by which we immerse ourselves in the diversity of Life as it is presented to us. All forms of life are participating in this dance, or song that life is presenting to us right now, in this very moment. 

Spiral dynamics is a way of understanding the ways in which we move through form in our life. Understanding spiral dynamics can help us by giving us a context for constant “leaving behind” of form. We encounter this “leaving behind” with the death of every passing moment. We experience the great rebirth with the emergence of the ever-present moment.

Spiral dynamics is the way by which, as we circle back on ourselves, we find ourselves immersed in a deeper consciousness. When we give ourselves permission to follow this winding path, we eventually integrate all those forms that we’ve left behind. And not just the forms that we ourselves, dear reader, have left behind, but all the forms that our evolving consciousness, on every branch of the tree which we are so graciously grafted into, has ever participated in. In other words, this is a pretty big deal (the Author smiles with you, dear reader).

For instance, when I was in my early twenties, I had an inner-awakening. Because of personal desperation and brokeness caused by the natural trauma of life, I met my Self in a deeper way. The way I came to understand myself to be participating in this awakening was in a fundamentalist, Christian, born-again experience. 

This spiritual awakening came to a contracted and fearful young man in the bible belt of Oklahoma, where fundamentalist Christianity was what the circumstance of our evolving Life was offering. 

This young man embraced his experience for exactly what it was, he took it in for all it had to offer. It was a joyful experience. It was a life-giving experience. And in the midst of this experience he communed with the great What-Is. He communed with the great I AM. He made an agreement with this Spirit within himself. he asked that Spirit to take him all the way. He offered his life to Life and he asked Life to live through him. He prayed fervently,  “Please take from me my life when I don’t have the strength to give it away to you.”(Third day song, maybe give it a listen, dear reader. It was this young man’s form). 

Yes, dear reader, This young man sat at the piano, singing and playing with his whole heart, “burn me up, Lord. Burn me up,” he beseeched the Lord. And in these prayers he was joining himself with the One-ness, recognizing the deep evolution of consciousness that he had seen in the Christ, the One he called Jesus. Just as the Christ’s disciples had done over two thousand years ago, this young man fell deeply and hopelessly in love with the Anointed One, that Universal Man, that Parable from Nazareth--That one life whose depth had touched humanity so intimately, so profoundly and intimately, that the energy of this Universal Man still found root in the heart of this individual being in the bible belt of Oklahoma. The Universal expression of love that he found in the good news of Christ took root in the heart of this young man

This is a common story. It is happening every day in our world. We are born into a new form. We say yes to the form. We follow the form to its inevitable death, the same death that Christ foretold in his own being. And, if we allow it, we transcend that form, and we move on to deeper levels of being. And it is here where having an understanding of Spiral dynamics may become important. Because it is the very essence of Spiral Dynamics which the Christ understood so very well as he watched Life being lived through his own self. 

Our friend, Ken Wilbur would say, that the experience of this young man was all true, but it was only true as far as truth of that form would allow him to go. Therefore, dear reader, in order to embrace the life of deeper truth, the form in which we once knew truth to exist in must pass away.

In other words, those prayers moved the young man. Through those prayers, G_d began moving the young man upward along the dynamic Spiral of Life. It’s really a very natural thing. It can be quite gentle if we allow it. But, we usually don’t, dear reader. We usually feel some obliation to fight this natural progression. We fight because we are so scared. We fight because we have been traumatized. We fight because we are convinced of some innate lack in our very own beings. We contract in fear at the death that is trying to liberate us from our suffering.

The push of life, that birth canal through which we all find ourselves passing, was also delivering this young man to a deeper state of consciousness. Moving to higher levels (or deeper levels if you like) requires a death process. There is a leaving behind of the old, an exchange of the wine skins. A seed must go into the ground and die in order to become the tree. 

This is the death and rebirth process that the Christ modeled for us, the story by which my particular history allows me to accept in this way. Your story, dear reader, may be very different, but you may allow yourself to see this common thread of death and resurrection in the tree. The seed is simply placed in the ground, by whatever course of events. The seed goes into the ground. It dies. It begins to grow. It begins to express the very DNA of its own being. The story of Christ was offering this young man a framework, a context around which to experience all the loss and suffering and confusion that was coming. All the loss and suffering and confusion that so naturally comes as we are recovering from the sacred gift that we were all given. Our sweet, sweet, trauma.

Yes, dear reader, I am once again reminded of our dear friend Andy Dufresnes. The prisoner who chiseled out of his cell with the tiny hammer (the tiny rock hammer that his friend Red had smuggled in for him). This death and rebirth process asks us to leave everything behind in order to move to the next stage of development. This is what it means to sell everything and buy the field. This is what it means when the rich young man comes to Jesus and asks, “Lord what shall I do?” and he says, “sell all that you have and give the proceeds to the poor, then take up your cross and follow me. Pick up this form, Son. It will break you for sure. And the death you die because of it will contain within it the life that you are looking for. But it’s not until the seed goes into the soil and dies that it can become the tree. Do you see, Son?” The rich young man so often walked away confused. 

Isn’t that how the story so often goes, dear reader? We find ourselves pushing away from our death in a desperate attempt to save ourselves. We don’t know how to work with this pain, do we? The pain shuts us down. We are not living. We find a thousand ways to distract ourselves from the death that so wants to find expression in us. Do we not, dear reader, very often find ourselves trying to save ourselves from the very death that was meant to bring our resurrection? 

But the Christ showed us a different way. The Christ showed us the path of a sweet Surrender.

Everything that we love must be forfeited. Including, according to the gospel of Luke, the love of mother, father, wife, husband, and self. And also, according to some translations of these verses, one must even hate one’s self before truly coming to Christ. Ask yourself, dear reader, is this true for you? Is this how you find yourself coming into the absolutely all-inclusive open arms of Christ in this moment. Are you in touch with, dear reader, this deep hate that you have held for yourself?

These words are for those of us who are just out of reach—those of us who cannot be held by the form as it now offered to us. These words are written for those of us who are imprisoned—those of us who are out of touch with the soil. These words are written for those of us who so desperately need to be sown back in to the soil so that we can die our very own blessed Universal Death! 

This is my story, dear reader. I find myself here with you, desperately praying for a resurrection in my life. We leave our forms behind dear reader, even when that form is our self. That poor, sad, resentful, traumatized being. Is she the one that you hate, dear reader? Or is she the one who is hating? We spiral back around. We transcend our form. We begin to live a resurrected life. And in that moment of resurrection, we say “yes” again, and the entire process is renewed again within us. 

All form can be loved, then left, transcended, and eventually integrated. That’s the beauty of the spiral dynamics model—the beauty of what the Parable was teaching us two thousand years ago. Those things that we loved and left, they come back to us, they are integrated into our consciousness. We may not be in touch with that at the time. But, that’s the reality that Christ was in touch with. That’s the reality that allowed him to suffer and then say “yes” to those who were hurting him.

It is in this way that our consciousness gains depth. We are made rich by the forms of our past as we continue to move upward into the infinite multi-verse, the great evolution of consciousness. I hope, dear reader, that you are able to see the beauty in all of this.

It is in this way that I have returned to the Christ. The Christ that I forsook, just as Petra did. It was Christ’s innate understanding of Spiral Dynamics that allowed him to be who he was. She is not the devil that we thought we needed her to be. Please, Great Mother, will you show yourself to us now. Help us to see. Please, Great Mother, help us to not fear you and the death that you bring to graciously bring to the self. Whatever is false in us, please take it, Mother. Whatever is not genuine, please burn it up. Whatever it is in us that is having such a hard time passing through, will you please reabsorb that into your being for us? Dear Mother. Please hold these Daughters. Please hold these Sons. Mother, we are hungry. Mother, we have been hurting. You know us, Great Mother. You know where we have been. Please make your presence known among us.

“Yes, Dear Ones,” cooed the Great Mother to her newborns, “I am here. Do not worry. I am here. I am with you. You are not alone. Let my light shine on you. Let my light shine from within your very being. Here I am. I am in you. I am everywhere. You are loved. You are held. You are my own. I am yours. When you don’t know your Self, you serve me. When you know your Self you are Me.”

It was at this point that our deep western yoga of science brought us to the edge. There we stood looking over this gaping chasm of the quantum realm. “It doesn’t behave the same down there as it does up here!” we hollered at eachother across the gaping hole that we’d just discovered in a Universe that we thought was absolutely governed by Newtonian Physics. “Nope, that’s not how it works,” said the German man who’d spent his life riding light beams through the depths of the observable Universe. “No. that’s now how it works,” he said, “You see, it is very disturbing to me as well, but you see, this is how it is: When one particle is affected over here, then another particle which somehow shares an invisible connection with her sister is instantaneously affected on the other side of the Universe, and this communication takes place instantaneously as I mentioned before…faster than the speed of light. You see? It’s spooky. I don’t like it myself. But this seems to be the nature of our reality.”

The man went forth into his day giving thanks and praises to his Lord and Savior. The joy of his salvation was restored unto him. He sang in the field where his great treasure was buried. The joy of his salvation was returned to him.

The man continued in his preparation for his journey. He folded laundry, treating every shirt with love and respect, speaking to each one and reminding them of the memories that they shared with him. 

There was the sea turtle shirt, which had come from the big island of Hawaii, where his family had gone on their last family vacation. With the shirt came a vision of two turtles, on male, the other female. They rested in large tidal pool. The male was still. The female swam to and fro in the pool. Young girls jumped in after her. The surface of the water was rippled in patterns by the Pacific breeze blowing in from the blue.

There was also his Blackwater Draw Boys three-quarter-sleeve, which was born from the love that he made with those boys from that band years ago, those deep and powerful boys of the Eastern High Plains who made such a thunderous sound for a brief moment.  Praise the boys of the Blackwater Draw.

And then there was this comfy two-tone blue fleece that he’d had for over twenty years now. She just kept asking to be worn. The middle-aged-man realized his love for this shirt, a form that would eventually pass.

He packed these shirts in his suitcase in preparation for his journey. He packed his socks. He packed his underwear. And he packed his favorite pair of pants that he had worn the morning after he’d taken that “lethal dose” of mushrooms, lethal in the sense that he was afraid that he would not come back. He’d had heard of people not coming back. He’d heard that sometimes it took a while to come back. Hospitalization possibly? That’s what he had been most afraid of that Christmas morning--A psychosis like that.  He didn’t know for sure if all that was true. But, the fear was real that he’d felt. It was the dose that felt lethal, that in the very least caused him to feel as if he were going to die.

The man tidied the great living room. He put his things away. He cleared the house for Dan’s guests who were scheduled to arrive tomorrow. The man made his bed. He folded all the blankets. He arranged the altar that he had constructed in his closet months ago, where he had burned sage and rang his singing bell and meditated. He then prepared a grilled cheese sandwich and some tomato soup for a late afternoon meal. 

As he prepared the meal he asked God, “How will I live? Is there a plan? What will I do when my car insurance is due? What will I do when the child support is due? What is the plan? Is there any way that we can plan together? Are you into that kind of thing.”

All the man’s energy was going into keeping himself in a right mind. He was using all the tools that he had acquired over the years in his spiritual readings, from his psychotherapy sessions, his musical skills, his writing skills, His yoga. He was experiencing some kind of flow today. There was much effortlessness in the way he moved from task to task. But then he got tired. 

He wondered if he was living at the speed of life. He knew that the writing he was doing was helping him. As he wrote about his experiences he was encouraged. Writing was one way that the man was renewing his mind. He was witness to the miracles that were taking place in his own heart as these stories were opening up to him. As he allowed the wisdom to come forth, he saw his story in a different light. He felt that he was performing the miracle that Stephen Schettini had asked of him several years ago. Stephen Schettini, the non-theist monk who asked the middle-aged man for a miracle. “Ha,” he thought out loud, “A non-theist monk asking for a miracle. Was that not a little miracle in itself?”

There are no little miracles, he reminded himself. All miracles are equal, and all flowing from the One Source of Love. All Praise the great mother of the Course! She whose name was not known until after her passing from this world, Helen Schucman. Praise be to the great Mother of wisdom.

Day 10 
12: 39AM

The middle aged man, the son, the father sat, facing North once again. Samuel Barber’s Adagio for strings played in his ears, the sacred sound of his resurrection. He sat in his mother’s home, which in the previous hours was filled with the joyful sounds of his growing and grown children, those children who had arrived at his house early that morning bearing gifts, Christmas gifts which they had brought to their father, the man who had walked away from their mutual home just twenty months ago, the man who now lived at the Adobe style house with the Saltillo tile, the man who now sat facing North on his mother’s couch which had been turned into his bed for tonight.

The adagio ended. He sat. He breathed in the silence. As he read through the first chapters of his draft he was overcome by two things:

1.	 the gravity of the Presence that he was discovering in this process. He found himself in communion with the All.

2.	 The immensity of work that the draft would still require in order to prepare it suitably for you, dear reader. 


The man arose from his seat on the couch and moved about his mother’s home. His Children were sleeping in the two spare bedrooms. He got the couch in main living room. 

Do you see the man walking about his mother’s home. Yes, he is seeking out a quiet place for communion. It has been a big day of travel and conversation. He seeks a quiet place. 

The man repositioned the floor mat in the bathroom. He lowered himself to his knees. He kneeled deeply. His body folded, his head partially on the cold floor tile. He allowed the I AM to be, or rather, he witnessed the I AM, the Being-ness of this consciousness. 

The man was grateful for this form which, in the past, he had called the water-droplet position, sometimes imagining himself a drop of dew resting on a blade of grass. His mind, of course, wandered, but the pose reminded him of his intention. 

Yes, der reader, as he awoke from the wanderings of his mind, the pose reminded him of the possibility of simple-being. The man kneeled on the bathroom floor in his mother’s home that Friday evening. He kneeled in all gratefulness for what he had experienced during the course of the day. He was in communion with the great What-IS.

The gifts that his children brought to him that morning made him very glad. His children stacked the gifts on the kitchen table in the Adobe house on avenue Q. He opened the smallest gift first, as it was at the top of the pyramid. It was small and light. 

“It’s a zippo lighter,” he said jokingly. 

The small package was actually much lighter than a zippo lighter would have been. The father tore the paper and opened the tiny box. Inside was a small piece of unusually shaped and stained-wood. The small piece of wood had a hole in the middle big enough for his middle finger. 

This was a minimalist gift, given to him by his son, its purpose--to hold the pages of a book apart as the reader held the book in a single hand. The father, knowing the difficulty of reading in bed while trying to hold open both sides of a book with two hands understood the importance of the gift. And as he sat on his mother’s couch now, turning it over and over in his hands, he was grateful for the gift from his son. He was grateful for its simplicity. He was grateful for its function. He was grateful that his son knew that he loved to read. He accepted the unusual gift. He loved his son.

The next gift was housed in a significantly larger box, it was from his youngest daughter. “Oh, I know exactly what this is,” the father said. “But I’m not going to say,” another attempt at a joke. He loved to hear his children laugh. 

As the lid came off the box, he saw a treasure trove. There was a wood patterned capo, just what he had asked for when his youngest had inquired about what he wanted for Christmas. There was a guitar strap decorated with golden suns. And, the gift that most impressed the father, held in it’s own cloth bag, a gorgeous leather bound journal, which looked like it was deserving to carry a sacred message. 

Facing his youngest daughter, the father held the book out in front of him in both hands and bowed. “I present to you the new gospel,” he said in a lofty tone. This time his children actually laughed and the father was well pleased. His youngest daughter had often impressed him with her generosity. He was powerfully moved by her ability to find gifts that mattered to him. He was grateful for her thoughtfulness. He was grateful for her.

The next present, the largest box, had functioned as the base of the Christmas pyramid. The father casually reached out to pick it up but it was very heavy. He repositioned himself so that he could lift the dense package from the table. He tore the paper from the cardboard box which was neatly taped shut. 

He remembered that his pocket knife was clipped on to his right pocket. He grabbed the pocket knife and flipped it open, as he had learned to do as a young police officer. He cut the tape and opened the box. Inside was something that he had mentioned to his oldest daughter that he wanted while they made the cheesecake to accompany their Christmas taco-Tuesday meal. It was a weighted blanket! The daughter had already, in fact, ordered it for him as they were preparing the meal together. The eldest daughter and her husband were well pleased with themselves, as they should have been. 

Once again, in an attempt to be the cause of his children’s laughter, the father removed the weighted blanket from its packaging and proceeded to lie down in a supine position right there on the hard kitchen tile. He pulled the blanket up o his chin, and his children did laugh with their father, and the father was very glad indeed.

The father had not expected his children’s gifts to bring him such joy. And so it came to pass that the family, having completed the exchange of their Christmas gifts piled in their two little blue cars and headed for the home of the children’s grandmother.

The first several hours of the journey were covered by dense fog and light rain. The oldest daughter rode with the father with her father. The Prince of Egypt soundtrack played as they drove (It was one of the current soundtracks of his eldest daughter’s life). And so it was that the father and his oldest daughter drove East, that day toward Oklahoma City on the same roads that the father had hitchhiked  two weeks before, listening to music that contained the story of Moses. And the father heard his own story in these songs. And the father laughed and wept for joy as he saw his story in this Universal story. And he heard the depth, and darkness, and mystery in those melodies that day.

The father was able to share the depths of his heart with his daughter that day, and his daughter had a heart to hear her father, and the father was very glad. And the daughter, although she was generally a very quiet person, also shared her heart with her father. And the father felt more known by his daughter. And the father also felt that he knew his oldest daughter a little more.

The daughter shared her grief at her father’s timing in the leaving of his family, for the father had dissolved his own marriage just one month prior to her own marriage. The father asked for forgiveness that he had hurt her in this way. He asked her how he could make it right. The daughter said that she was no longer angry, although she had been very angry with the him at the time.

The man and his children stopped to eat at Subway, all four of them, and they laughed at each other’s ridiculous jokes. It was a hearty laughter that resounded throughout the Subway in the gas station somewhere along the foggy highway which lead them East toward the children’s grandmother and their belated Christmas celebration.

He returned to the story of the writer who was enjoying lunch with his kids at the gas station sandwich shop. They paid for their meal. They were just emerging from the filling station into a cloud covered Texas panhandle parking lot.

His son sat in the passenger seat of the little blue car. Inspired by his new college experience, The middle-aged-man’s son spoke in elevated tones. He spoke quickly and with much energy.

“I’ve been reading some Richard Dawkins,” said the son, “He might not be as much of an arrogant ass as we thought he was, Dad. He’s really got some good things to say.”

The father was searching for common ground. 

“Okay,” said the father, “tell me what you mean.”

The son went on to discuss Dawkin’s book The Selfish Gene, published in 1976 but still required reading in a formal education on biological evolution. The father was proud of his son’s curiosity. He was happy that his son was able to enjoy learning. 

“The common spiritual ground that we shared a while back…I’m not there any more.” Said the son, “I’ve become more of a materialist.”

The son, like the father was being folded over in the blueberry batter, leaving form behind. 

“Well, I’m proud of you, son. You are growing. You are progressing. It’s okay if we don’t have that same common ground right now. I wonder what common ground do we share?”

The two men rediscovered each other through conversation, trying to make peace in this dynamic relationship between two dynamic individuals. 

“I’m worried about you Dad. I’m worried because you don’t have Mom to take care of you any more. Whose going to take care of you?” It was difficult for him to accept the father’s latest decisions to drop his nets and surrender to the flow of life. 

“I’m not ready to go with that flow,” said the son, “I’ve got too much to get done. I’m just not in that place. I’m in school. I’ve got a life to build.”

“I understand,” said the father, “We are at different stages.”

“I mean, I could understand if you were my age,” said the son, “Maybe I could understand you taking some time out. But, I don’t understand you doing what you are doing at this age. “What are you going to do? How are you going to survive? You don’t have anyone to take care of you now.”

“You know, son, when I left your mother I told her exactly that. I told her that it was time for me to learn to take care of myself. I think I’m in that process. I’m learning how to live in a way that suits me. I don’t have the answers to those questions. I wish I could tell you, but I just can’t. I hear your concerns. I am listening.” 

The father continued. “Son, I love you just the way you are. You don’t have to see things my way in order for me to approve of you. You have my blessing. I see you, and I like what I see. You are a young man. I see your heart. You are strong. You are powerful. 

He went on as he wanted to affirm his son, 

“You are building the container to hold the substance of your life (Richard Rohr, Falling Upward). You are in the first half of your life. I trust that you will find your own way. My father is a hurting man. He is a suffering man. Because of the years that I have tried to reconcile with my own father, I understand that the blessing I give to you today cannot be revoked. Even if I go crazy and try to take it back someday, this is the blessing that cannot be revoked. Do you hear me, son? It’s okay for you to leave our common ground behind. They continued their discussion as the father lead them into a discussion about spiral dynamics.

Praise be to the ancestors as they have empowered us in our journey up the great snake, the Great Serpent who spirals into the infinite multi-verse.

After several more hours of conversation between the father and son, the two blue cars diverged from the great toll road and onto Eastern Avenue. The Universal Mother was preparing for them a great feast. Crackers and cheeses were laid out on the island in her kitchen when they arrived. There were also nuts and grapes and candies available there on the kitchen island. The hospitality of the Universal Mother was palpable in all their hearts, and the son gave much thanks, for his heart was filled with gratitude. The joy of the son’s salvation had been restored unto him. The family rejoiced in each other’s presence long into the night.

A red meat sauce simmered on the mother’s stove, just as it had done long ago, when the son lived with her as a boy, long before the grandchildren were even thought of. 

“It all smells so delicious,” said the son to his mother, “I am so happy to be here with all of you!” he exclaimed. And he truly was.

The Mother made a sacred salad which contained a multitude of textures and flavors. Together, the grandmother and her oldest granddaughter prepared a tangy homemade dressing to compliment the green salad. The mother spooned garlic-butter over a sourdough bread which she then broiled to a perfect shade of golden brown in her oven.

Then he became very sleepy.

The son, giving thanks to his mother for the meal that she’d prepared, got up from the table (even without excusing himself as his mother had taught him to do, but still with much thanks in his heart) and found his way over there to the couch where he covered himself with the weighted blanket, closed his eyes and allowed himself to fall into a sleep as he listened to the laughing and talking of his family. The Children were happy, “maybe giddy,” thought the writer.

Good nights were said. The oldest daughter and her husband retired to their room. The two youngest children retired to theirs. The mother and her husband went to their bed too. And the son was left alone in a sacred space on his mother’s couch, this son who was making peace with a Universe who was out to help him.

And so it came to pass that the writer found himself sitting on the couch, the one who recounted all the joy that had transpired on that twenty-seventh day of December in two-thousand-and-nineteen, that year of our Lord, exactly one year after the middle-aged-man had admitted himself to the hospital and been transported by ambulance to Sunrise Mental Health Hospital in Roswell New Mexico. 

But, on this  twenty-seventh day of December of two-thousand-and-nineteen the middle-aged-man was not in a mental hospital. No, dear reader, he was feeling quite well. He sat with great joy, tapping out words on his Chromebook.

“There it is! There is the field that I bought so many years ago!” exclaimed the father-pilot. He described to his children how he had calmly piloted the plane, how he’d managed to ease the plane down (much like Sully did on the Hudson). “I managed to set her down in the very field that I purchased so long ago, the same field that contained the treasure,” the father proudly explained.

He explained to his two oldest that he was a disciple of Christ, and that he was no longer able to hold the form that their earthly father had maintained all those years. He was able to describe his sufferings in a way that they seemed to understand on some level. The father did not sense that he was justifying himself. Of course, he could not know what his children heard when he spoke. He could not truly understand what they saw when they looked at him. But, the father knew how he had come to the place where he was now. He knew exactly how he had arrived in that field, in all truth and in all honesty. 

The prayer that he had prayed at the cabin in the Lincoln National Forest had been answered. The man had seen the joy of his salvation restored. His heart was full of praise and thanksgiving. He was moving in and out of form. He sat now at his mother’s house in the quiet of the night, the children that he had raised and the husband of his daughter were sleeping in their rooms. His mother and her husband were sleeping in theirs. 

Although he knew exactly how he’d arrived in that field, he felt a satisfaction that had little to do with certitude. He sat with his fingers curled over the home row of his laptop. The laptop rested on the weighted blanket, that same gift that he had said that he wanted even after the gift was already on its way to his daughter.

The writer paused in his writing frequently. He looked around the room. A double sided fireplace opened itself to two separate living areas, one of them adjacent to the kitchen. His couch was located in the main living room where Marl’s great sports television and the leather recliners rested. 

The writer placed his hands together, acknowledging the Life that was being lived through him. He placed his thumbs on his forehead. He bowed his head toward his heart. He allowed himself to come back to the I AM. He gave room for Life to have its say through him.

The man was making peace with a Universe that was out to help him.  He closed his laptop, acknowledging the North. He placed his laptop on the small table by the couch. He went to the bathroom. He returned to the couch. He turned out the lamp. He pulled his weighted blanket over his body. He lay on his back and closed his eyes, giving thanks, giving praise, acknowledging the One Source. He allowed himself to rest. He allowed himself to be the great I AM.

The single drop of dew rested upon the wide blade of green grass in the morning sunlight. The yellow light of the sun appeared to emanate from the heart of the dewdrop’s center. In the perfect stillness of the morning the water droplet sat on the green blade of grass which sprung from the earth, rooted in the soil. They carried sticks, formed froth, tumbled playfully over small water falls, and sometimes splashed up on the edges of the bank, then sinking into the soil.

5:48 AM

A young man sat in his senior English class. At the head of the classroom stands Mrs. Hubbard. She is the only one who is interested. With deep gutteral conviction and twist of tongue, the dried lips on her weathered face recite the Canterbury tales. The seniors fall asleep. Saliva falls from the mouth of the weary young man as he wakes up from a nap.

But there is another day, a day when they are not studying the Canterbury Tales. Today they read Walt Whitman. Today the boy-man hears something. He understands. He saw it there. There it was, right there on the page, a meaning so deep that he would not stop repeating the line:

“I lean and loaf at my ease, observing a spear of summer grass.”

The single line of Whitman contained all he needed to know that day. He was moved. Or possibly, his constant anxious motion was arrested for a brief moment that day in his senior English class led by the aging sun-spotted woman. This woman who, day after day, conveyed her love, her passion for these words as she stood up there facing the class, risking the tying of her tongue and the shedding of her tears. Just minutes ago, the writer awoke with a start. He had a dream that he could not remember, but the powerful energy of the dream lingered. The writer paused now, closing his eyes, allowing the energy of the dream, which still lingered in his body, to aprehend him. “The writer paused now,” The writer repeated to himself, for it was in this sentence, “The writer paused now,” that he detected the Great-Turning, or the Great Folding-Over which he had first experienced in his mother’s blueberry batter, and which he had more recently become familiar with after he’d consumed the large dosage of mushrooms on Christmas day. And now he knew what it was that he had dreamed of. It was the dream of this Great Turning to which he awoke with a start when he heard his daughter open and close the bathroom door close just a few minutes ago. “There it was again,” thought the author, “The place where the past meets the present—that place where we perceive the past to be the present through the use of symbolic language?” 

“The writer paused now.”

A statement in the past tense which contained the present.

This reminded him of the Course In Miracles lesson that he’d read and practiced last night just before he went to sleep. “Let’s see, what was the lesson?” wrote the writer. He bent over. He reached down into the space between the couch and the coffee table to retrieve the thick blue book. He retraced the last three days:

Lesson 9: “I see nothing as it is now.”
Lesson 8: “My mind is preoccupied with past thoughts.”
Lesson 7: “I see only the past.”

The writer was reminded that by the time the light from the lamp reflected off the objects around him, travelled to his eyes, and was then processed and interpreted by his nervous system, there was a certain fraction of a second that had passed. What it was that he thought he was seeing now, was actually the past. Yes, it was this lesson that was taught to him once in a physics class. That lesson was taught in the past, that place that we have such a difficult time  escaping. That place where we just cannot help but go.

“The writer wrote now,” wrote the writer.

The writer, by his very nature, is the observer who comments on the past, no matter how infinitely close he may perceive himself to be located in the present moment. “Infinitely close,” repeated the writer to himself. This reminded him of a few lines of a  Rumi poem he’d read last night. 

He remembered that the poem was on page seventy-two and seventy-three of the book that he’d purchased yesterday while shopping with his children. He now felt around for the book between the couch and the coffee table. Was he feeling for Rumi, or was he feeling for the book? Rumi was the author who died so that his reader could live. In his poems his reader found his own life-- Rumi and Hafiz, those Sufi poets who recorded their love affair with the Eternal Now.

The spirit of Rumi Spoke in tongues:

“The moon has opened its face
And its wings made of light.

If yours cannot.

Night and day an arrow comes toward you

The writer reached now for the thick blue ACIM book. He practiced his lesson of the day:

“I do not see this book as it is now,” he said.
“I do not see these hands as they are now.”
“I do not observe these thoughts as they are now.”

This writer—the dying author-- commented on the present which he wondered if he could ever truly be a part of. “Even when I am not writing, how close can I really come to the present? Infinitely close? like the arrow? Is this the purpose of the teachings of the Buddha? Isn’t this the purpose of the Vipassana practice?” The writer then paused and practiced ushering himself along in this present moment. His fingers instinctively paused, hovering over home row, allowing his documentation to be as closely in touch with the present moment as possible. 

The writer paused again, his hand was on the Rumi book. He grasped the book. The book: sacred written form which the Christ did not feel necessary to participate. He wrote no words. He was making contact with the people. Christ become a parable himself, his life recorded by others long after he was gone. Legend.

This was the hero’s journey that was now being revived in the writer’s own heart. “Can the parable write of itself?” The writer wondered. 

The writers’s eyes finally came back to Rumi’s living words. He reached across the coffee table to retrieve the Christmas gift he’d received from his only son, the uniquely crafted piece of stained wood with which he could hold a book open with one hand. He read the line about the arrow:

“Night and day an arrow comes toward you
From a hidden bow.”

The writer is transported back to a Spring morning in 1990. He sits in Algebra class. The classroom windows are cracked open. The infectious Spring leaks into the classroom. Birds build nests in the trees on the other side of the high school football field. Mr. Watters stands behind athe overhead projector factoring a binomial. Mr Watters is a fluid father of symbols. 

Two students walk across the parking lot. They each hold a cigarette in their hand. They will not go to any more classes today. Once clear of the parking lot, they stop and light their cigarettes. For a brief moment, they know true freedom.


The overhead projector fan drones on, a tanpura inviting improvisation. His students shift in their seats., sensing the truants freedom as they light their cigarettes. Mr. Watters attunes the break in his student’s attention. He moves his dry erase marker to the top-left quadrant of the overhead projector screen. Without a word, he draws the infinity symbol. Now, he traces the infinity symbol, over and over again as the infinity symbol so naturally invites. 

Obed Watters, projects the infinity symbol in real time on the screen. His job is to teach Algebra, but right now he pauses from the binomial to trace the symbol. The symbol is right there for all of his students to witness. The symbol has no apparent connection to the day’s lesson, but here it is. It is the only thing now in the students minds. The dry erase marker dances with the infinite. 


In another version of our universe which the writer imagined to be only slightly more dystopian than the one in which he now lived, Orwell’s thought-police enter Mr. Watter’s classroom door. They do not knock. Yes, it is the thought police. They come in and sweep up ol’ man Watters. 

Now they are taking pictures of the evidence. “This was an obvious attempt to infect the minds of the children under his charge,” said the lead inspector. 

“Was this an act of subversion?” the writer now questioned, “He seemed such a straight laced man! This man-of-Watters who traced the infinity symbol. Did he open up a hidden and dangerous universe for those boys and girls in the public schools?”

The overhead projector is still wet with the infinity symbol. “This dry-erase marker was purchased with state funding! This marker was purchased exclusively for the purpose of teaching Algebra II!” shouted the man taking pictures disgustedly. 

Old Obed Watters was mopped up. The students are pretending that they are not affected by this sudden intrusion. A gloved hand picked up the marker and placed it in a plastic bag. The high school Juniors sat nervously, waiting for a replacement teacher. They remained very still in their seats. The temportary teacher arrived just minutes after the removal of the excessively fluid Watters. 

The high school students did not mourn the loss of their teacher. They could not mourn as they did not yet know how much they loved him. The infinity symbol was erased forever from the overhead projector, Mr. Watters never seen again. The image however, was forever etched in the student’s collective Soul. That which points to the moon, will have its effect. And at least one of these students will love him one day.

That signifier was having its effect now in the life of the middle-aged-man. Yes, the symbol was having its effect as it pointed to uncountable possibilities in an infinite multiverse. The memory of the symbol penetrated the fabric of those young malleable souls who had witnessed the tracing of the side-lying figure-eight. 

The infinity symbol was not the only introduction made by Watters. It was the same fellow, the middle-aged-man’s Algebra II teacher, who had also introduced him to Zeno’s arrow. The arrow which, by approaching half the distance to its target with every movement, could never actually reach its mark.  The arrow may come infinitely close but never hit its mark. 

This was the same arrow, the writer now believed, that Rumi referred to—this arrow that “night and day comes toward you from a hidden bow.” Rumi asks his reader to surrender to the arrow of which we have no shield to protect ourselves. 

The writer now understood this impartation of Mr. Watters to be of the same variety as his vision of the blueberries—the blueberries that his mother (that Universal Glow) had taught him to fold (not stir!) into the batter. These are the modes by which the writer now understood Life to be communicating with him. This was The Great Learning, The Great Turning, the Great Folding Over, the way by which we evolve. This is how we move forward as a species.

We are not really a static species, you see. Things are not nearly as solid as we think they are. Thank you, Mr Darwin, for showing us this! There’s a way of looking at all life as a transmuting expression of consciousness, the same way that Special Ed, the Marxist, had taught the middle-aged man to see the thunderhead. Any one species, like the clouds or the dewdrop, is in constant flux, although we still feel compelled to reify that which is constantly changing. It’s how we desparately want our world to be. Unchanging. Change can be scary, and evolution presents to us a dynamic world.  

Do you, dear reader, recall those reified beans? Do you remember the Marxist—whatever that means—and the reified beans that he so slyly called the middle-aged-man’s attention to? Those reified beans, our neighbors just South of the U.S. border. Those ones which were alienated from their own labor. Do you remember the beans, dear reader?

It was the train tracks that did it, or so the Marxist said, and it was quite a convincing argument. Yes, the middle-aged-man had come to believe that it was the train tracks that did it—those train tracks that arrived from the North just before the turn of the twentieth century. 

You see, dear reader, the trains brought a great alienation to the land. Alienation, the most dreadful of all diseases. The reified beans were alienated from their own labor. Alienation, that disease of separation. That ailment which is the inability to see the All in one and the one in All. That disease which separates us from our own evolving consciousness. 

Praise be to Mr. Marx! Praise be to Mr. Ed, that sly Californian who brought his subversive impartation to the Eastern High Plains so that the middle-aged-man could add it to his collection—the infinity sign, Zeno’s arrow, the great thunderhead, the reified beans, the train tracks South, and his dear mother’s blueberry batter.

It did have a place. It had its place in this draft, in all its draftiness.

Exquisite Stillness

exquisite—extremely beautiful and delicate. highly sensitive and discriminating.

	My father is a very fearful man. Of course, he would never admit it. But his fear has eroded a deeply grooved path in his being. Like water which runs through a canyon, my father has no choice but to follow the course that fear has carved through the terrain of his inner person.
	My father has never learned that he is not exactly like his thoughts. He is completely identified with every thought and emotion that he experiences. That’s why he is so easily offended. If his thoughts or emotions are challenged he has no choice but to become defensive and angry.
	My father suffers deeply. But he has hidden his suffering so well from himself that he cannot understand why he feels the way he does. Because he cannot ease his own suffering he must blame people and circumstances for the way he feels. 
	Just last year I asked my father to come and help me. I was going through a difficult time with a recent divorce. My kids weren’t speaking to me. I was plagued by suicidal thoughts. My father was very helpful.  He helped me to make the home where I was staying livable. When I asked him for money that he didn’t have, he became very angry, telling me, “You are the reason that I am a bitter old man. I have dreamed of putting a bullet in your head. And I have dreamed of putting a bullet also in the head of your mother.” His eyes were red and tearful and full of rage as he pointed his finger at me from across the table. Although I was also suffering, I was able to ask him to forgive me for the pain that I had caused him.
	My father does not have friends. He told me that he has intentionally pushed people out of his life and that he experiences satisfaction when his birthday passes and no one acknowledges him. He has also told me that he is hurt when no one acknowledges his birthday. He has said both things to me. I think I understand how both can exist in separate moments.
	It is difficult for me to relate to my father. I know that if I challenge his thoughts and emotions there will be conflict. It seems that merely presenting my own experience challenges him, so I often just let him talk and talk about the way he sees the world, knowing that it will be easier if I just stay quiet.
	
	I am beginning to see how I too, have lived in fear. I am beginning to see how my suffering has injured others. I am beginning to learn how to give myself the compassion needed to allow my fearful thoughts and emotions to dissolve. I am no longer blaming people and circumstances for my own suffering. Now I hope to stop blaming myself and find an entirely new option.
	
When I was four years old I watched the movie Jaws. The ocean, I understood, is where fear resides. But that’s not really how it is. Fear resides in my own mind. The ocean is just the ocean and sharks are just sharks. I understand now that there is some remote possibility that if I go into the ocean that a shark might eat me. But if I allow my fear to dictate where I go and what I do, then I may never go into the ocean and play in the waves.
	When my children were young, we took them to the ocean for kayaking. I and my oldest daughter, Anna, became seasick. Our guide, Max, suggested that we jump in the cool water to relieve our nausea. I felt sure that as soon as I jumped in the ocean that I would be eaten by a shark, but I jumped in anyway, and so did my daughter. I did not want to pass on my fear to her.
	
	This weekend I went on a solo backpacking adventure in the Pecos Wilderness of New Mexico. As I was signing the trail register, I noticed someone had written a warning about cougars. “Stay together!” they wrote. I was by myself. There was no one to stay together with. As I set out on the trail I felt like prey, scanning the mountain above and below for movements of large cats.
	After seven exhausting hours on the trail, I pitched my tent, made myself dinner, and built a large fire. The crackling warmth of the flames made me feel safe and secure. It was the first time I had ever been in the wilderness all by myself. I went to sleep watching the campfire from the tent. Two hours later I awoke suddenly. The fire was out. It was dark. There was a mysterious clicking sound close to my camp. I was terrified.
	I lay there for some time, hoping that I could fall back to sleep, but I could not. I finally sat up in the tent as straight as I could. I listened to the strange clicking sound. A light rain began to fall on my small tent. The sound of the raindrops hitting the tent just inches from my head was unpleasant. I startled with fear when the logs in the fire shifted suddenly. My brain started inventing other reasons to be fearful, but panic was not an option. I was miles from anyone or anywhere. No cell reception. No help. no comfort.
	I recalled my meditative practice and then I calmly prayed. I focused my attention on my breath. I realized that no matter how unpleasant the sound of the rain was, I could not change that. I accepted that I was vulnerable and alone in a dark forest with only a thin layer of fabric between me and the wild. I had no control over any of this. The only thing I had any chance to control was my response to fear.
	Eventually the rain stopped. I recalled something I had read earlier that day from Pema Chodron. She had encouraged me to move toward my difficulties instead of trying to push them away. I wondered, “What if I get out of this tent and just sit outside in the dark?” I allowed myself some room to make friends with this idea. Part of me was resistant, but another part of me thought that that might be okay. Minutes passed. As I opened the tent, the sound of the zipper seemed to echo throughout the canyon. I found my sandals and then I sat again, waiting for the courage to go out into the dark, closer to whatever threats, real or imagined, might await me. As I finally emerged I could see the outlines of large rocks and trees. I sat on a large stone by the extinguished campfire. I could still feel some warmth emanating from the darkened coals.
	As I stared into the dark forest, I allowed myself to become aware of my breathing. Thoughts came and went. I imagined a sudden piercing howl. I imagined that Golem was creeping around on the rocks just outside my camp. I imagined that a large cougar was stalking me, skulking down the mountain in preparation to attack. But, every time a thought came I allowed myself to return to the stillness that was all around me. I told myself, “none of these imaginations are actually happening.” What was happening in my surroundings? Stillness. The mysterious clicking had stopped. The rain had ceased. There was absolutely no wind. I was in the middle of a profoundly still forest. Exquisite stillness.
	When I allowed the stillness between my thoughts to align with the stillness of the Pecos Wilderness there was harmony. Stillness within. Stillness without. As the fears came I understood that I had a choice. I could allow my mind to entertain fear, but then I would be missing what was really going on. So I just kept coming back to the stillness, and when I did that, there was no fear. I had no control over what might happen in the next moment. But that was really none of my business. I was much more concerned with what was actually happening, this Exquisite Stillness. I was eventually able to return to my sleeping bag.  I slept until the sun rose.

	Hiking down the mountain is often much easier than hiking up. Me and my son Joseph have hiked together a number of times. He likes to consider all that potential energy that we store up in our bodies as we are hiking up the mountain which is now being converted into kinetic energy as we make our way down. 
	I made my way down the mountain to my little blue Toyota with a cracked windshield. Still sensing the release of this kinetic energy as I drove home from my solo backpack adventure, I called my father. I wanted to talk to him about how I had felt in my role as potential cougar food, because I knew he would understand. He loves to think about the terrors of being eaten alive. Our conversation was the impetus for the words you are now reading.
	I have lived for most of my adult life powerless to control how I respond to fear. My fears were so deeply imbedded that I didn’t even understand that they were fears. I participated in psychotherapy; I joined churches; I prayed; I had demons cast out of me; I went to AA meetings; I exercised; I studied; I tried to be a loving person; I became an atheist; I meditated; I became a feminist; I had intelligent and caring friends; I listened to my wife; I went back to school and got a better job; I wrote songs; I performed music; I got standing ovations; I did many things to try to fix myself, but fear continued to dictate how I perceived the world. Even when the forest was still, my brain was inventing fears.
	I want to be careful here that I don’t sound like I have the answer, but if I am truthful, I feel like I do. I will try to explain. Today the answer for me is acceptance of what-is, and confidence that a power greater than myself is able and willing to restore me to sanity. When I am in the dark forest all by myself and my brain is inventing a half dozen reasons that I should be scared, I now know that I am not obligated to follow these story lines. If I am willing to look inward toward this Exquisite Stillness, I can experience a profound shift in my perception, a miracle of perception change. Today I am willing to experience a deeper Reality than I was able to conjure for myself. If I allow it, this deeper Reality will flow from within me. A well has been unstopped that I had allowed to be clogged by all of my fearful suffering.
	All of those things I said about my father, those things are true about me too. And if that is the reality that I choose, I render myself powerless, bound to my fearful story lines. 
No matter how hard I tried, I could not think myself out of my inherited mental illness. But today something has changed. Today I have a reprieve from my insanity. Today I am focused on this Exquisite Stillness.

…And so the first story of the mountain was told by the middle-aged-man, the story of the Exquisite stillness. This was the story of a man who had been trying to make peace with his father for a lifetime, and the story of a father who had also been trying to make peace with his son.

And this is how the writer, the one who was sitting at his mother’s home in Oklahoma City, came to witness again the long journey up the mountain that he had been making over the previous year. For it had been three-hundred-and-sixty-seven days since he had driven his little blue toyota, the one with the severely cracked windshield, to the Emergency room instead of going to work on that December day. It was just over a year since the middle-aged-man found himself walking the circular hallway of the psychiatric unit in Roswell where he had received the prayer of restoration from the One called Clinton (that Universal Crossroads), the gay black man who had interceded on behalf of the man, the man who had just had another cavity search, the one who had just prayed, “God, please help me.”

But there is still another mountain story to be told, dear reader. And the dying author is very much looking forward to the possibility of sharing that story with you. The story of how a man flew up a mountain with a feather and was rocked in the arms of a an evergreen.

8:03 AM

And so it came to pass that the writer prepared for his journey to Bentonville, where he was to meet with his two new publisher friends. He sat in the red and white checkered chair by the large windows in his mother’s living area adjacent to her kitchen. His mother emptied the dishwasher. His eldest studied her part for her lead role in a French comedic opera. His youngest was mischievously interacting with the world as usual. His son slept. The man put his arm around his son-in-law.
 
Leaving early would give him a chance to visit the art museum that his mother had been recommending to him for years, his mother, the Universal Glow. “Am I idealizing my mother? Maybe, thought the wildly talented writer. And also, maybe I can meet with my old friend Van Gogh today, that one who struggled in this world, that one who tried so desperately in his relationship with light to make peace with this swirling cosmos, that one who painted the starry starry night. Our Dear Vincent who truly did paint the divinity that he witnessed. The one who passed down to his brothers and sister the vision of seeing life that way.

It was with deep trust and affection for all that-is that the writer, somewhat hesitantly left his joyful family that morning. He left them in Love. He left them with thanksgiving in his heart.

The windshield of the man’s little blue Toyota was iced over. He needed a tool. He started the engine, turned the heat on high defrost, and picked up Dickey Lee Erwin’s CD case from the middle console. CD cases can make good ice scrapers when its not too cold and the ice is not too thick. The process did not take all that long. Soon he was back in the driver’s seat.

He put the car in drive. He used the neighbors driveway for a turn-around. As he passed house after house in his mother’s comfortable neighborhood, he was reminded of the mandolin that he’d left behind. His guitar was with him, but his mandolin was not. As a prayer of willingness to listen, he turned the car around. He parked the blue Toyota in his mother’s driveway, went inside, grabbed the mandolin, said another short goodbye to his family, then passed over the threshold of his mother’s home again. 

He found the Rucker Brother’s CD, the album that he had written and produced with his old friend from music school. The album spoke to him of hope, his friends last name, Matthew Hope. The man continued the journey on his own, giving praise for the sense of purpose that he felt in his being, giving thanks for the clarity in his mind and soul, giving thanks for death and the resurrection that he witnessed in his own being,  He picked up his phone and accessed its audio-recording app. He raised the phone to his lips.

The traveller spoke the following words that day as he scooted down the Oklahoma turnpikes in his little blue toyota, stopping to pay the tolls along the way.

I believe he is praying for us…“I pray that God would keep us rooted, right here in this moment, the eternal now, moving at the speed of life. Gratefulness in these hearts. Thanksgiving on these lips. Peace. Peace. Peace to you, my dear reader.”


Maybe following Life is like foraging as a hunter gatherer—seeing the nuts and the berries, following the herd of animals as they migrate. Maybe it’s more like that than obedience to military General. 

The writer, the middle aged man, the dying author, this traveller, held his phone close to his face and spoke into the audio recording app. He reveled in the idea of his words being captured in real time as he drove down the road. He passed a sign for Braums, a fast food restaurant. He had worked there as a soda jerk in his twenties. It was his first job after he and his wife had sold all their possessions and poured those drinks out in the winter wheat field. 

The traveller tapped his brakes, dropping the little blue toyota out of cruise control in order to stay with the flow of traffic. “I’m just moving at the speed of Life,” he happily reminded himself out loud. He was on interstate 244 East heading toward downtown Tulsa.  

Tulsa OK, the city in which a young man and his wife spent their first married evening. The traveler took the Joplin exit where the road forked. He laughed in recognition of the binary. Yet, in that moment his forward motion did not cease, for he did not wish to cause a traffic accident. His GPS told him that he had sixty five more miles to go until the next fork in the road.

He passed the Bartlesville exit. Bartlesville, that town where one of his old friends was from. Kevin, the gifted guitar player. Years ago, a young man and his friend Kevin were musical partners. Kevin was the one who had a heavy correction for the hitchhiker sitting there at Denny’s waiting for a ride. 

Kevin, the man who had spent six years in prison--six soul crushing years in a federal prison. How does a man process that kind of suffering? How does one learn to survive in places like that? Where one can hardly ever feel safe? Where one cannot masturbate in private? 

“What the fuck are you doing?! You’re not some kind of fucking hobo. I mean, what the fuck are you doing out there on the goddamn highway? You’ve got responsibilities! You need to take care of your business.” 

This was how Kevin’s voice arrived in the middle-aged-man’s ears as he sat at Denny’s, his hitchhike coming to a conclusion. With as calm a voice as he could maintain, the middle-aged-man finally said, “with love and respect, Kevin, I’m going to hang up the phone now.” He had not heard from Kevin since.

The traveller took a moment to make his heart right toward his old friend. He took a moment to allow this miracle to happen in his own heart as he drove through downtown Tulsa, the place where he and his wife had spent their first married night. 

Today, the man felt his own company, and it was good company. And the man felt the company of you, dear reader, as he drove on those elevated interstates. “fifty eight miles to the next fork in the road,” a large green sign informed the traveller. 

He marvelled at the joy that was in his heart—this pure, simple, clean, light-hearted experience. He knew that if a word search was done on this manuscript, that the word “experience” would certainly be the most used. “That’s appropriate,” thought the writer, “considering where I came from. Considering that album made by the twenty-something year old Jimi Hendrix, who’d asked a fourteen year old boy that question, ‘Are You Experienced.’” At eighty miles per hour, the traveller laughed out loud. That fourteen year old boy took that question into his heart. “Are you Experienced?” That fourteen year old boy took that album into his heart. He took that creation into his heart. Noel Redding on Bass. Mitch Mitchell on Drums. Yes, that music captured that fourteen year old boys heart. It was the boys father who had made that introduction.

With fifty-four miles before the next fork, he breathed in the joy of life. He breathed in all of the connection that he was sensing. He rested in the weave of life. The first time he took the medicine, that’s what he had seen. He saw the fabric of being. He saw the fabric of community. And he saw himself supported in that fabric. Yes! It was more than sight, more than seeing. With the help of the medicine, the middle-aged-man was able to experience a felt sense of being supported.

It was then that the traveller was able to acknowledge fear in his own heart. “There it is. Right there,” he said. “Fear, I acknowledge you.” He felt the fear in his chest. “Fifty one miles to the next fork,” he announced. 


Yes. He felt the fear in his heart—a fear that maybe he’d missed it. Fear that maybe he hadn’t worked hard enough. Fear that he should be at work right now in the physical therapy clinic. He braked abruptly, almost passing a state trooper doing sixty-five in a fifty-five.

I have played and replayed that memory for myself many times throughout my life. I can’t really be certain of much surrounding that memory, but that’s the story I just told surrounding the birth of my brother. That is the evolving memory that came to signify his birth in my mind.”

The narrator. The observer. .
The one who tells the stories. The one who simply is

The one who we were with before we took that wrong turn back there, dear reader.

The audience does not want to be told about the character. The audience would rather experience the environment for themselves, they want to be there as the story unfolds,and the best way for this to happen is by allowing them to feel the world through the character’s senses. The dying-author awoke just before the dawn of a new decade, a dawn that had already cracked on much of the world to his East--A midnight which had already come to many of his fellow human beings.
