His hands were a little too big and clunky, but it was only a problem for a moment, because he’d been practicing for a lifetime for this moment. And it was then that the greatest non-performance of his lifetime had occurred. The non-performance that would restore the joy of his salvation. The non-performance in which praise and thanksgiving and (dare he say?) worship flowed from his being. He praised the sun in the sky. The trees and the soil. The birds and the grass. He prayed for the people in the passing jet as it left its trail through the blue.

And it was in this same spirit, grabbing on to the form he knew, this time with an instrument that he did not know quite so well (Lina, his mandolin) that he began to sing again:

“mine is a story of redemption
I once was lost but now I’m found
I’m letting go of my pretensions
I’m dancing to a deeper, higher sound
We are the oneness, we are the unity
We are the light

And so another vamp began… “we are the light, we are the light, we are the light”

And the son rode the wave of energy that the Spirit had been teaching him how to create all these years. 

And then his song changed to a minor key. And another vamp began in which he recalled the journey of the last year of his life, from the time that he arrived at the psychiatric unit until he had a renewed serenity experience in conjunction with his 12 step work.

And he faced North, looking into his reflection that was made in the large window in his mother’s living room adjacent to the kitchen. And his mother was witness to this song. And the mother was witness to the thanksgiving and praise and the testimony that flowed from her eldest son. And when he was finally done she said, “Amen. Are you sweating?”

And with that the son laughed with that because he now had the gift of not taking himself too seriously.

And so it came to pass that the son shared with his mother the story of his baptism in the cold mountain stream and his climb to the top of the mountain just outside the Lincoln National Forest.





“Father?
“Yes, Son?”
“Can we climb that mountain?”
“Yes, Son. Let’s climb it together. One step at a time.”


Day 18
8:35PM

The man allowed himself to be drawn out of a dream as he was awaking from a nearly three hour nap.

A strange thing had happened. He had just received a text from the only man that he’d ever confessed his attraction towards. It was a man that he’d met at the first treatment center that he’d attended. The writer was unable to dismiss the text as merely coincidence. He had not heard from the man in over a year.

The writer had fallend asleep hours before praying for direction. “Have I gone past the point of no return?” He asked the Universe. “Is it time to go back home tomorrow?” he prayed out loud.

He felt as if he’d done some kind of violence toward himself earlier that day as he had forced himself to stay at the church service that he’d attended, the church service that his mother served at there in the Bethany Children’s Center. 

He went because he was curious about his mother’s life. He went because his mother invited him. He went knowing that it may not be his cup of tea. He went with the intent of honoring his mother, whatever that meant.

He’d sat in a darkened conference room watching a live-streamed broadcast of a church service that was taking place across town. He watched Sandi Patti, a veteran of popular the popular Christian music world, deliver an impressive musical stage performance. He watched as an intelligent, funny, and attractive middle-aged-man preach about patience. He allowed himself to eventually sing with the other’s who’d gathered in the dark room to watch the images projected on the white screen. He allowed himself to laugh and the preacher’s jokes. 

After the service he found his car in the parking garage. As he was situating himself in the driver’s seat he got a text from Dan. He and Christy had gone to Las Vegas. They got married. This was marriage number eight for his good friend, Danno. The middle aged man hoped that his friend found what he was looking for this time. The middle-aged-man certainly had found the crazy-wisdom and love that he needed in Dan.

However, the middle-aged man also found his already uncertain future to feel threatened. He was now living with a married couple, which was a very different thing than having a single man as a roomate. The man put these emotions on the back burner and continued with his day. He and his mother had been invited to lunch.

The middle-aged-man offered to help clean up after the church service. The middle-aged-man politely and even vigorously accepted an invitation to a meal that his mother’s dear friend prepared for the mother and the son. The son retrieved his guitar from his vehicle and played pre-mean instrumental music for the lunch party.

Despite all of these efforts, the middle-aged-man felt false and contrived. He did want to offend his mother or his gracious hosts, but he was bored as her sat there in their polite company, being as polite as he possibly could. He also felt that any attempt that he made to express his genuine self would only end in confusion, a confusion that he did not want to bring on himself, or his mother, or his mother’s friend and her husband. 

He ate two pieces of breaded tilapia. He ate the lavender peas. He ate the seasoned wild rice. He ate thickly buttered Hawaiian rolls. He devoured two helpings of cobbler and ice cream. After lunch was over and there was an appropriatley long pause in the polite conversation, he announced that he was scheduled to teach a guitar lesson across town. He excused himself from the table, gathered his coat, latched his guitar in its case, hugged his mother and his gracious host, shook the dentist’s hand, and found his way to his little blue Toyota.

The food weighed heavy in his stomach and he could feel a heavy sleepiness weighing on him. He was unsure how he would give of himself as he made his way North across OKC on Rockwell Ave. But the middle-aged-man made his way none the less. 

The city finally gave way to fields and trees. He turned West on 192nd and shortly arrived at his old friend’s beautiful home. The home that his entrepreneurial friend, Brian had built himself. The middle-aged-man had played a limited role in its construction. He’d worked for his friend back in the late 90’s at his screen printing shop.

The middle-aged-man struggled with feelings of inadequacy (or was that jealousy?) as he entered the luxurious home on the Western edge of Edmond. He was aware that his beard may appear to be scruffy of unkempt. He was conscious of his little blue car and all its inadequacies. 

The man remembered the ACIM lesson the day: “This thought about _____ is not a neutral thought. The man had been aware, even as he had been travelling north on Rockwell for the last twenty five minutes that his thoughts were far from neutral. His thoughts were contributing to the “illusion” as ACIM said. Even as he was aware of this he prayed that God would use him in service. And it was in this condition that the middle-aged-man arrived at his old friend’s house because he volunteered to give his friends gifted son, Nash, a guitar lesson.

He was greeted by Shelly and another son, Hudson, who was also interested in guitar. The middle-aged-man did the best with the energy that he had. He struggled to find a way for the three of them to make music together. He used his musical skills to engage the boys in the music. They laughed. They played. The middle-aged-mans efforts were not without fruit. He was able to impart som musical wisdom. He used his skills to serve the family. The middle-aged-man felt pleased in the effort that he had been able to put forth.

Shelly inquired about the wellness of his children. The middle-aged man was happy tht he could report that they were indeed well. The middle-aged man shared in a limited way about his own life. The boys inquired about his recent backpack journey, which caused the middle-aged-man to feel insecure in that he was possibly bringing some unwelcomed influence to these growing boys.

Lots of ego. That’s what the middle-aged-man was trapped in today. He wasn’t quite where he wanted to be. Or was he not quite where he needed to be? And if so, where was it that he was truly needed? Was he somehow on this day being less than true to his Self? Had he not chosen to be exactly where he was?

Nash introduced his bearded guest to the family’s Christmas present, a knobby tired go cart with an impressive sound system. “Get in,” said Nash. The middle-aged-man complied. Do you like “Smile?” Nash asked.

“I don’t know what you mean.” Said the man.

“It’s a song. It’s called “Smile. It’s one of my favorite jams.” And with this Nash turned up the volume and began wildly circling the terrain of the property, the man holding on for his dear life and smiling indeed. This young boy seemed to be intentional in the lifting up of the middle-aged-man. They circled the large property several times, Nash leaning forward in the seat, mashing the accelerator to the floor, the middle-aged man pushing himself down into the seat with his arms, smiling some more.

There was a gentleness and a wisdom in this family that the middle-aged-man felt somehow estranged from. There was a distance that their obvious financial success caused in him. He did not want to feel the alienation that he was experiencing, and he did not blame any of them for causing it. It simply was.

He’d felt the same as he’d sat earlier at the large table, eating with his mother and her friends. He felt somehow out of place, like if he spoke up and really became himself that it would just be too much. 

After the middle-aged-man said his goodbyes to Shelly and Hudson, who had begun disassembling the Christmas tree (Christmas decorations! a task which the man had recognized in himself as some kind of emotional trigger for years) Nash very deliberated showed him out to his car.

Nash lingered with gentle affection for the man. He hugged him, and hugged him again. He showed the man how to do the a handshake that, in his current state, he found to be very challenging.

“Promise me that I’ll see you within the next year,” said the boy.

“I don’t make promises,” said the man.

“Well, promise me that you’ll come back in the next two years,” the boy compromised.

“Nash. Next time I’m in town I will get a hold of your Dad, okay.” 

The boy expressed some kind of affection for the middle-aged-man that he was unable to generate for himself that day. The man had no idea how a human could have knocked on the door of his heart more effectively. This boy was present in a way that the middle-aged-man could hardly understand. He tried to receive the gift. It was his intention to receive this gift from the Universe.

As the young man finally allowed him to close the door and drive away, the middle aged man prayed. “God, I offer myself to you. God help me. God help us all.” He was exhausted. He’d been up writing for most of the night. He made his way East on 178th street as the fields turned into the city streets of Edmond.

His exhaustion turned into desperation as he found himself seemingly unable to navigate his way back to his mother’s home. He found himself, against his will, consciously passing the intersection of 143rd and Coltrane. An intersection that he recognized immediately as the entrance to an old world. He made a U-turn and turned West toward one of the neighborhoods of his youth.

The man could only feel pain and loss and regret as he drove his car through this neighborhood. He paused in front of his old family’s house on 143rd. The small tree that he, as a boy, once climbed was now thick and towering. “That was thirty five years ago,” the man marvelled to himself. He could not understand how it was the same tree. The man could only feel loss and suffering. He could only cry as he turned back to the North on Foxbriar Drive. 

He travelled down the hill that he once coasted down on his red ten speed. He passed Steven Koch’s house, the kid with the coolest Diamond Back bike in town. Tears formed in his eyes and his breathing stopped as his body tried to allow the anguish of his youth to surface. He passed the house where he had hurled racial slurs at one of the only black children at his school. The middle-aged-man felt sick and lost. How could this even be the same place. How could he know it so well and yet also so alien?

He wanted to stop and beg the parents in the park to hold him. He wanted a chance to go back and do it again, this time with somone who could hold him. No. None of those words were doing it. There was nothing. There was no sentiment that could say what he felt. These were all just constructions with which the writer attempted to express the sickness and sadness that seemed to color the youth of the middle-aged-man.

The man felt fragile, and he knew why. This morning he lay in bed trying to accept that which was unacceptable. After his shower, he’d had an intimate experience with the water droplets and he had allowed himself to think thoughts that had never been acceptable. There was a tenderness in his being that morning. And then he’d asked himself to go out in to a world which he still perceived to be unaccepting. A world which he could only perceive himself as being separate from. He was seeing the world still through the eyes that he had inherited from his father. 

This was how his father felt. This was why he lashed out in fear. This was the world that the young boy had inherited. This was the vision of the world that had been passed down to the boy in his genetics. And this was how the middle-aged-man saw the world today.

The middle-aged-man passed by the elementary school that he’d attended from third to fifth grade. The low hanging sun prevented him from getting a good look. He continued this long detour, struggling to find his way back to his mother’s home. 

Was that hunger he felt? Probably not. But he passed a sushi restaurant and that’s what he wanted. Nash had handed him several twenty dollar bills before he’d left. He parked his car and went into the sushi and saki bar. He sat at a table. A man approached and offered to serve him. The man felt guilt. He did not have the money to be here. There was child support. Ther were his children. He ordered something off the menu to-go. He sat with his head in his hands at the table. There were only two other people in the restaurant. Why could he not allow himself a meal here? 

He took the yellowfin tuna out to his car, unsure of what to do with it. He ate a piece in the parking lot. He was worried that if he took it home that his mother would think he was spending his money unwisely. He brought the fish into his room, drenched them in soy sauce, and sat in a hidden corner eating the raw fish and carrots and pickled ginger and green onions. It was a hidden and guilty meal. He now felt hidden and guilty.

And this was when he noticed the text from Ted. 

Ted, the man who he’d found attractive as he attended the same treatment center at which he’d met the woman from Bermuda. The same treatment center at which he’d admitted to a room full of people for the first time in his life that he was a bisexual. The term seemed clunky to the writer as it sat on the screen. Bisexual? What the fuck does that mean?

“How the fuck can you finalize a life experience like this with a word like that? Thought the middle-aged-man. ‘bisexual?’ ‘Gay?’ How could a lifetime of pain and confusion be solved by these terms that seemed to be charged with the same insanity that had plagued the man for so many years. Was this anguish going to be solved by sleeping with a man? What the fuck? The middle-aged-man did not think so.”

The church service. His mother. Her friends. The well-to-do family with the caring son. How is it that all of these people and situations could carry so much pain for him. How is it that he found himself here today? 

While visiting his old neighborhood, he drove by another old friend’s house. There was the driveway where he had first asked Christ to come into his heart, where he had asked for a new life in the Spirit. There was the driveway in which he hoped he’d solved this problem once and for all. There was the driveway where he came to understand that everyone is born into sin, but we can receive a second birth in the spirit. There was the driveway where he first understood that he could be born again.

And so it came to pass that the young man of twenty one (or was it twenty two years?) came to ask the Lord Jesus into his heart. And it was on that night that the man’s friend, the Christian saxophone player, opened up the bible to the book of Romans, chapter 8, from which somehow the young man understood that if some kind of pledge of allegiance was made to the one and only true God, that he would no longer have to face that which was unacceptable in his own being, that part of him that was magnetically drawn to his fellow guitar player that night that he’d run away to the bathroom to splash cold water in his face. 

And it was on that night that he drove away from his friends house with the knowing that nothing would ever be the same again. And then the young man met the woman who had also repented from that which she had found unacceptable in herself. And it was upon this faith that Jesus had delivered them from their sins, that they were new creations now in Christ, that they got married and had three children and went forward into life with all the strength and devotion that they could muster.

The writer sat facing Eastward, reclined in his mother’s northern-most spare bed, the weighted blanket and the chromebook in his lap. He could hear his mother and her husband in the kitchen. It was 10:33. They would be going to bed soon. He did not know if he would be staying another day here. He placed the chromebook to the side and swiveled out of bed.

It appeared that the mother sat waiting for the son to enter. They spoke to one another for quite some time. The son shared his heart. The mother was accepting. It was that simple. The son felt sheltered in the mother’s acceptance. The son felt safe in the mother’s home. He was free to stay if he needed to stay. He was free to go if he needed to go. The mother accepted the son. The son felt the mother’s acceptance. There was room for healing in the acceptance that the son felt from his mother. They hugged. She gathered her things. She went to bed. It was fifteen minutes after Eleven.

The son made himself a cup of tea in the typewriter mug that the mother had bought in recognition of the son’s writing efforts, an herbal lemon. The son showered, not because he was especially dirty, but because it felt good. He lathered with the peppermint soap. He shampooed his thick hair and his greying beard. He rinsed. He squeegeed the heavy glass door.

He positioned the prayer mat facing the East. He gave thanks to the One living Being. He sensed the being in himself. He and the Being were one. It was that simple.

He thanked God for the richness of his experience. He thanked the Father for all that he’d witnessed as he had occupied this particucular form. He rose to a seated position on the mat, scooting the mat under his naked bottom to avoid the cold of the tile floor. These quiet moments of clarity were precious. He acknowledged the sanctity of life. He acknowledged the wisdom in his being. He acknowledged the great I AM.

He brushed his teeth. He retired to his bedroom for another rest. 

Day 19
9:00AM
The middle-aged man found himself packing. The middle-aged-man found himself preparing a sandwich for the road and some of the home-made caramels that his aunt had given him in Kansas. He packed a banana which he knew he probably wouldn’t eat because he had the caramels. He packed a package of Belveeta crackers, orange cranberry flavored. More than enough food for his six and a half hour journey home.
The hatchback of the little blue toyota stood open in the street as he loaded his car, the windshield frosted over from the cold and moisture of the night before. He loaded his guitar, his mandolin, his suitcase, his books, and his writing tools, including his trusty chromebook, which he’d purchased months ago on a hunch that he would need it. 
As he scanned his mother’s house for his things, he discovered his mug on the kitchen counter—the mug that his mother bought for him with the typewriter on it to celebrate the writing of these words. On three yellow post-it notes he wrote a note of gratitude to his mother and her husband, thanking them for their generosity and their hospitality, their love, their acceptance. 
And he asked his mother, in the note, to please tell Sebby, the next door neighbor boy with the powered scooter how much he’d enjoyed making his acquaintance.
Having packed his belongings into the little blue toyota he got on his way.
He passed under the Rockwell Ave bridge as he travelled West on the turnpike. “Exact Change Only,” read the sign, only after he got on the turnpike. But that was okay, because he had exact change today thanks to his mother and father, who between the two of them, had provided him with just enough change for the turnpike to last his entire stay.
He had come with his children, listening to the Prince of Egypt soundtrack with his Eldest daughter two Fridays ago. He’d had a lovely time with his children and his mother celebrating Christmas. He made the trip to Bentonville to visit those two that had encouraged him on this writing project, those two who had encouraged him in the writing and in this journey of healing. That day in Bentonville, Arkansas where he did not expect to meet Sapphos of Lesbos. Harbor Dave encouraged him to work on his dialogue. Eileen had encouraged him to yield to the spirit of Life which flows through all of us, the Universal Eileen, the one who had sent him the string of words which moved him as powerfully as any other string of words ever had.
He brought his children to meet his father at Louie’s at lake Hefner where he’d been served moldy black brocolli. He stayed two nights at his father’s house, going to the place that scared him, once again, giving himself to the trauma ceremony that his father chose to live over and over again in his own being. But this time during the ceremony he had blessed the father who had given him so much. He blessed the man who had also taken so much from him. Although he grieved deeply again the loss that he’d experienced in the most recent attack from his father, the middle-aged-man felt quite certain that the father had no power to take anything from him ever again.
The middle-aged-man stopped to pay the toll. The coins jingled into the large plastic cone receptacle one at a time. The toll light turned from red to green. He pushed the accelerator toward the floor. The car moved forward. He rolled up his window. This was the last toll that the middle-aged-man was required to pay as he left the city.
As he accelerated through the on-ramp he remembered the prayer of his hurting inner-child. It was a prayer that had emanated from his very own heart just hours after his father attacked him again, “Please, don’t make me go back. I don’t want to go back ever again. Please, don’t make me go back.” The man knew that his heavenly father made no requirements of him to go back again. The heavenly father—the being who demands nothing. The one who sees and acknowledges. The one who gives the blessing that cannot be revoked except by one’s ego. The middle-aged-man’s earthly father tried to take his blessing back once again. The father tried to replace the blessing that the son had already accepted. But the middle-aged-man was now more certain than ever that this was not the way of things.
ACIM was teaching him that there were no neutral thoughts. A thought is either contributing to the teachings of love in his life and in those around him or his thoughts were contributing to the strengthening of the great illusion of fear and separation. Today as the midle-aged-man payed his last toll with the money that his mother and father had given him he knew that he was not required to return to his father’s home ever again. And so, once again he accepted the gift, the ceremony, the only ceremony that his earthly father was able to give him. 
As he continued on the turnpike he approached the exit to his father’s home. Or maybe he had already passed it. “Maybe I already passed it,” chuckled the middle-aged-man.

 The sun was still rising in the sky. A red GMC Sierrra passed him on the left. Yes, it was true, he had passed the exit to his father’s home without even knowing it. The exit for I-40 West drew near. A slight movement of the steering wheel to the right turned his car once again in a westerly direction toward the beloved muse. He felt a relief as he merged into the traffic on I-40, that great interstate that bisects the large metro area of OKC. Garth Brooks Boulevard approached, one and a half miles ahead. Garth Brooks the famous singer who graduated from the same highschool as the middle-aged-man. Garth Brooks, the performer who people had always asked the young man if he’d be the next of—“Are you going to be the next Garth Brooks, son?” people asked as the young man played his latest songs. “I don’t think so,” the young man would say, the question perplexing him somewhat.

“When you write songs” said the middle-aged-man, “When you dedicate yourself to song writing people often listen to your songs and tell you what it sounds like to them. It’s difficult for a young man growing up to write songs of his own. It’s a beautiful challenge to try to find one’s own voice. A gift to watch one’s voice develop and to eventually find a voice that is an authentic and somewhat original sound. We are all informed by the songs that have been written before us. Any original sound or original idea is perhaps worth dying for.”
And so the writer found himself having come full circle back to the original email that he’d sent dave and Eileen and Dave (Dave and Eileen), the one in which he was reminded that the Christ never wrote a story of his own. The one in which he was reminded of the author whose name he could not remember, and fittingly so because the message of this author was that in order for the reader to experience her own birth the author must find his death.

Garth Brooks Avenue came and went. The middle-aged-man found himself in the flow of traffic in the westward moving lanes of interstat 40. The same road that he’d travelled well over seventeen years ago now as he made his way to the little college-cow-town, singing the song that went like this: “Maybe I could ride straight through to my destiny—like a highwayman the best of me seems to be on the road where my future’s laid wide open.”
He remembered how Stephen Schettini had asked him to do a miracle, the reformed buddhist monk, the non-theist, if that is really a thing, had asked him to do a miracle.  And so in the name of the great Love, the reality, the true nature of being, the man once again accepted the miracle that was coming to pass in his very own heart. The man knew that his being could not be defined by any one label or any word, be that a medical diagnosis like ‘bipolar disorder’, or be that one of the words from his youth, “fag” buttfucker, homo…those words that had been spoken with such disgust, those words that were created in fear. The man knew that he had no obligation to take up any words. He knew that he had no obligation to make any promises or pledges or even….the man knew that he was incapable of re-inventing himself, for he had done that innumerable times. As the man drove away from the great crossroads in the heartland of the great nation which lay on one side of a great irregular sphere which hurtled through the expanding universe, part of an interconnected solar system in balance which was in turn connected with a greater galaxy, the milky way, which was in turn in relationship to how many other billions of galaxies? Yes, as the man drove away from that one very tiny crossroads in a vast multiverse he was connected to the source. He was connected to a deeper power, a greater purpose. It was his intention to live a full and rich life. It was his intention to continue to live this full and rich life in which he was already engaged. It was his intention to say yes to a universe that was out to help him.

His mother had come in to say goodbye that morning as the writer sat in his favorite reclined position facing the east, the direction of the innocent sage, the trickster, the sacred fool. He told her of his plan to visit Bruce, of his hope to experience a deeper healing than the bible belt had to offer him. His plans to possibly leave this country, even if it was just across the border for the first time in his life. Her eyes appeared nothing less than concerned. “I don’t know what to say,” she said.
“That’s okay,” said her son, “You don’t have to say anything. You don’t have to do anything. You’ve done everything just right.” They hugged, the mother and son. She left for work. The man’s yellow elk skin gloves rested in the passenger seat of his little blue toyota with the cracked glass that his youngest daughter had nearly pushed out. The cracked windshield that his daughter had nearly pushed out of the frame. His yellow elk skin (praise be to that great mother). The gloves that had kept his hands warm as he sat so many days ago waiting for a ride that would never come in Amarillo as he first tried to make his pilgrimage to Oklahoma City.
He’d given up on that pilgrimage as he settled his external fram kelty in the booth at Denny’s. He found a place for his large cardboard sign and mandolin. He received a call from his young friend Jerry, as he decided to be honest in his moment of despair as Jerry said, “I’m worrie about you, are you okay?” The hitchhiker confessed that he was ready to come home and he found no shame in himself tht day as Jerry came to pik him up. He allowed himself to move in a direction with as poor a plan as might be appropriate sometimes. With as little forethrought as he could allow himself to not have. As he writer continued west on I-40 he remembered the man that he’d met at lake Hefner, the man who cared for the feral colong, the man whose voice the tiny cat with the matted hair who breathed with much distress had emerged from her little cat house to greet the kind and gentle old man.

The old man also asked the middle-aged-man if he was okay, to which the middle-aged-man replied, “yes, I’m Okay. Thank you very much for asking.”

Miracle after miracle was happening in the man’s life. Miracle after miracle of self-acceptance and self-love and inner exploration. Miracle after miracle of kindness and generosity, nurturing, compassion, the great turning was turning over and over in the life of this individual. The macro univers contained in the micro-univers. The micro universe expressed in the macro. And yes, dear reader, the man was lingering. The middle-aged-man lingered in your company for he did not want to say goodbye.

Dear reader, this gentle man does not wish to part company with you. What the middle-aged-man knew that this real time writing experiement could not go on forever and ever. It was time to begin ediing. It was time to begin looking at the creation that had been born into this world. It was time to give it the love and the care that it needed in order that you, dear reader, might eperiences it in its fullness. And so it came to pass that the writer said one more farewell to you, dear reader, a farewell that was never really a goodby as long as dying-author and reader held one another in each other’s hearts. There was still one short story to tell. A story which the writer had seen coming for days and days now. A story that the writer thought he was going to tell two days ago which he ended up telling in person to his mother first. A story that once again he found himself holding himself from in his reluctance to release this project, in his reluctance to release this exhange, this interaction that he was not having with you, dear reader. The writer breathed in. the writer breathed out as he allowed his final story to come.


Day 20
4:11AM
Early the next morning, the writer reestablished his North-facing writing-center at the great marbled island in the adobe home. The three ACIM books and his old bible once again supporting his chromebook as he faced the large mirror. 
He fed and watered his growing African violet and the thick-stalked basil plant that his mother had given him last summer.
He played several songs on his guitar and doodled in E major for some time.
He placed the three pillows in front of the sink, where it was his custom to retreat when faced with the binary.
The writer allowed himself to pause in this space before writing any further. He continued to linger in what he felt to be the concluding moments of the real-time writing of his project. He was aware of an anxiety in his being this morning.
The day before, as he traveled West on I-40, he stopped at a great cross which towered on the horizon just south of the interstate as he approached. It was advertised on the preceding billboards as some kind of crucifixion rest stop. He needed to pee, and he was interested. There were other places he could have peed. He wanted to pee there.
He parked his car in the gravel parking lot. He made his way past statues of Christ and those he’d encountered on that fateful day of his crucifixion. He made his way up a great entrance where a  life-sized bronze statue of Jesus stood amidst a great flowing fountain. The middle-aged-man found the entrance to the gift shop. He entered.
He walked into a large sweet-smelling room packed with items that he judged would mostly interest the fundamentalist Christian. A woman who reminded him of a librarian emerged from a back room. “The bathrooms are that way,” said the woman, “We are glad that you are visiting us today.”
The man used the restroom. He emerged from the bathroom, surprised to meet himself in a mirror just as he opened the door to exit. It surprised him. He wondered if it was placed their intentionally to somehow surprise people. As the man met his own bearded image in the mirror, he felt that maybe he was meeting the Christ in this gift shop. The man perused the items in the gift shop, wondering if he could find anything that spoke to him. With a surface scan he found nothing that resounded with him as Universal in nature. The man was on guard, obviously, half-expecting to be overwhelmed by a spirit of fundamentalism against his will.
He stepped out of the gift shop without encountering the librarian again. He approached the great fountain. He gazed upon the figure of Jesus standing in the midst of the flowing waters. The man felt utterly exhausted. He was grieving the incident with his father. The man leaned up against a man-made great stone pillar. He found himself a participant in the glory of what had been created here, this homage to the living Christ. The magnitude of this creation was truly impressive and he found himself wrapped up in the love and the dedication of the hands and hearts that had erected this great monument to the story of the life that was lived over two-thousand years ago.
He found himself leaning against this man-made stone structure asking God for further assistance. He found himself participating in a form which would have once been taboo to him. Just two years ago he would have only allowed himself to deconstruct and criticize what he now gave his heart to. One last time, he focused on the welcoming Christ who stook in the midst of the flowing waters. He then returned to the statues which encircled the gigantic white metallic cross. The statues were dwarfed by the looming white, behemoth. 
The man allowed himself the luxury of non-judgment. Yes, he was aware of all the reasons that he might allow himself to discount this monstrosity, but his judgment was suspended just enough that he was present. He was participating.
He approached the first station where a statue of the Christ stood facing pontias pilate who sat on a throne. The Christ gazed at the Roman ruler with surrender in his eyes. He would make no justification for himself. He and his friends were making deep love to this world. And, the Christ knew that his own death would be the orgasm that planted its seed in the womb of consciousness. 
The cross was placed on the back of the Christ. He willingly carried it. He met people along the way. A man named Simon helped him carry the cross when he grew weary. He saw his mother too. He asked her for her witness. He asked her to see into a deeper reality. He asked her to see her son as the Universal. He asked her to experience his death as the death that would give the world insight into the true nature of reality—the seed that goes into the earth and dies and becomes a tree. He asked his mother to see the spiraling serpent that was the staircase by which consciousness ascended and eventually integrated all forms below. “Please mother,” he said, “don’t’ try to stop this. This is what I came to do. This is what I came to reveal.”
And so the journey of the Christ continued until he was laid on the ground in a supine position on two large pieces of wood. Nails were driven into his hands and feet and he was lifted up in between two men who were also suffering deeply as they watched their life passing away from them. 
One of these men accepted the great What-Is that he was experiencing in that moment. This man looked upon the One who hung beside him and saw his brother. He gave himself to the same process that the Christ was willingly surrendering to, and in so doing, he made peace with himself and all that was. 
Another man that hung beside the Christ was unable to accept the suffering. He was unable to make peace with the nature of reality. He was unable to accept his own death. He was unable to reconcile himself to the great What-Is, that which is happening right now which we have no control over.

And so the Christ, in his deepest moment of suffering, In this moment when it truly felt to him that his father had forsaken him, he called out. He cried out in that moment of deepest despair, giving thanks for the life that he had lived and all the people that had loved him and all those that he had loved.
“Thank you, Father. You are a good Father. I am suffering Father. My hands and feet have been nailed to this tree and my body is suffering deeply. I feel humiliated, Father. I have been kicked and beaten and stabbed. So many have left me and I feel so alone, Father. Please, Father, I do not know how much more of this I can take. I am having difficulty breathing. I know that things are not nearly as solid as they appear to be right now, but I am hurting. I am hurting so badly. I feel alone, Father. I am looking at this world and it truly appears very dark to me. I am terrified, Father. My body is quivering and fear is racking my consciousness. It is difficult for me not to ask now what it is that I have done wrong. What have I done to deserve this, this is the question that I prevent myself from asking right now. My being is now filled with the sickness of these “others,” these people who have seen the great love that me and my people have made to this world. These people who witnessed our great love and now are tyring to destroy the great love that we have made. I have now become the witness to all the great suffering in this world. I have now become the suffering that these people have brought upon themselves. I am folded in Father. I do not know how I will come back. I am losing my mind, Father. How long will this last? How long can I feel this without turning on them, Father. How long can I experience this without hating myself, without despising the very suffering that I have become? I feel as if Life itself is punishing me. I feel what they feel. I feel absolutely alone. I feel absolutely scared. I feel absolutely separated, and my flesh is pulling on the nails at my hands and feet. My bones are grinding now against the hard nails and breathing is excruciatingly painful, Father. Father, why have you forsaken me. What have I done to deserve this separation that I now feel from you? Why am I all alone? Father, I am dying now. The light is changing colors, Father. There is nothing I can do to save myself. This is really happening. I am fading. Please, Father. Hold me. Hold me, Father. I just want to be held now, Father.”
And it was in that moment of deepest despair and suffering that this Universal man, as death was overcoming him, made peace with everything that was. It was in that moment that he accepted the true nature of reality. It was in that moment that he made peace with his own death. And it was in that moment that his death became the Universal story of all death. It was in that moment that he accepted all that was. It was in that moment that, as his body continued trembling and quivering in its death throes, there was an inner peace that came upon this man. As he made peace with his own being in this way, he was able to say:
“Father, Forgive them. They don’t know what the fuck they are doing. And that’s okay. It’s actually understandable, considering the big picture. Things are just as they should be. Please forgive them, Father. Please forgive them. I am done here. I am the seed. I am the One. I am the One who is crucified. I AM. The rising Christ. 
And so it came to pass that the middle aged man found himself sitting on the steps convulsing. Sobbing and crying with the pain of the interaction with his father just days ago. So it came to pass that the man had said ‘yes’ to his own death as he had approached his own earthly father. And the Son was free to grieve without any shame. He was the only person at the crucifixion rest stop that windy day in the Texas panhandle. He checked periodically to see if there was anyone pulling into the gravel parking lot. But there was not. So there he remained for quite some time, giving himself to the grief. 
The Son was finally able to give himself to a grief that was free of shame and self-condemnation. The Son had finally seen his father for who he was. The man was now a five year old boy. The five year old boy now understood that there was not anything he could say or do that would make his daddy love him. There was nothing he could ever say or do to make his daddy happy. The five year old boy saw that his father was a hopelessly lost and angry soul who could only blame others for his own pain. The five year old boy was free at last. He was free to grow up. He was free to be himself. He was free. 
Having cried all the tears that this location could contain. The man rose. He walked along the path to the tomb, where the stone was rolled away. He entered the tomb and he lay in there for a time, awaiting his resurrection. When it was time, he rolled over and sat up. He greeted the angels who awaited him. His hands came together and he raised them to his forehead. He bowed toward his heart. He took a selfie. His eyes were red and moist with tears, his body exhausted and aching. He took a picture of the tomb’s exit, hoping that it would remind him one day of this time in his life.
He returned to his little blue car. Started the engine, placed the transmission into reverse and listened to the gravel crunch beneath the tires. There was a night-deposit prayer-request box on his way out. He found his receipt from the Oklahoma City Zoo lying in the passenger seat. “Pray for healing,” he wrote on the receipt. He half-stumbled out of the car and placed it in the prayer box.

He accepted the energy for exactly what it was. 
He sat there in the waiting room with the sound of the television and other noises which came from a game that a little girl was playing on her mother’s cell phone. The little girl’s father bent over in request that his wife massage his neck. The man saw the suffering of life in this little family. The man saw his own suffering in them. He phased in and out of thoughts which jumped back and forth between love and fear. He continued to choose love.

Having tended to this practical matter, he left the doctor’s office and resumed his journey. As he rolled into the college-cow-town he called his friend Ron. Ron invited him over. The middle-aged-man walked through the doors of the two aging artist’s home, the yellowing temple of music and hanging creations fashioned from items that people had thrown away.
The middle-aged-man recounted the highlights of his trip to Oklahoma city—his time with his children and his mother, the painful visit with his father, the many life-affirming meetings with old friends. Yesterday, after he’d taken the medicine. After he’d set himself free of the burden of real-time documentation. In the back yard, after he’d crunched the frozen grass with his bare feet. After a great chilling rush passed through his body. There was a ceremony that began. 

The man approached the small bridge that crossed a dry man-made stream bed. It was the little stream that fed the pond where the squirrels and the robins drank.

He sat on the warm black bridge as it had been covered with some kind of protective black rubber covering. As he came to a seated position, he noticed that there was bird shit on the bridge. He became curious about the bird shit. At first glance it looked terrifying to him, something that he did not want to look too closely at. But he allowed himself to get real close to it. He saw the partially digested seeds. He saw a white mucous which enveloped the green chalky meat of the shit. He remembered what he’d written on the first page of his ACIM. His little mark of wisdom that he’d left there for himself and whoever would read the book in the future. “Even the most nutritious of foods eventually becomes excrement.” Selah

What once looked good to eat. What once fed us. What once was delicious, eventually passes through our bodies and becomes shit.

“Yes, thought the man sitting on the bridge. How we deal with shit is most important!”

His boss, Fheb had once told him about how when she grew up in the Philippines they did not have toilet paper. She described in detail how they dealt with their shit with bear hands and a bowl of soapy water.

How did the Christ deal with his excrement? How did Hafiz and Rumi deal with their excrement. 

The writer had special wipes with which he could deeply clean his sphincter after a good shit. These men had no wipes. People in the past must have been much more deeply in touch with their excrement. Surely, this little thing must be a big deal. How do we work with our shit? How do I clean my ass once the body has purged the food that was once good to eat. How do I invite this food into my body for nourishment and how do I purge that which is no longer desirable.

In this was the heart of spiral dynamics, realized the writer as he sat looking at the bird shit on the bridge. We embrace form. The form passes through us. The microwave beeped three times, announcing the readiness of the meal. Thanks be to God for the food we are about to receive. Dear reader, please help me find my way now. Pray again for my death that you may live. Pray for your own restoration. Pray for you own wholeness as I pray for you now.

“God, I pray for the reader now. I pray for the ones who have accompanied me this far in our journey. I pray for a deep recovery and a healing. For surely anyone who has read this far into the blasphemy is also leaving their self behind. Surely anyone who has read this far is also experiencing the great turning. Yes, dear reader, You are with me and I am with you.

As the middle-aged-man left the blessed cabin in the Lincoln national forest that day he gave his travels to the Great Spirit. He blessed the Owl Woman. He blessed the Universal Stan (the one who brings us all together). The gravel crunched under the tires of the little blue toyota with the severely cracked windshield that his daughther had so perfectly destroyed in a seizure.

The man stopped to have a visit with the two burly bulls, the orange and the black. The man communed with the Christ in the bulls. He had given himself to the Christ in the turning around of his car. He had given himself to the spirit of Christ that he found in his curiosity.

The man gave himself to this great turning around. He gave himself to the willingnes that was arising from within. It was in this way that he found himself under a cliff face yelling in the direction of God, “Make me a disciple! Empower me to follow! Make me a disciple! Empower me to follow.” The middle-aged man turned in every direction in supplication. 

It was in this way that he found himself singing a song that he’d composed that was simply the contents of the gospel of Luke Chapter 14


 Great Crowds of people

He sang this song as he invited God to empower him to follow. A great heart memory of sonship came back to the man. It was a memory that had been deposited in his body but had been latent. He felt the sense memory returning. He felt what it was like to be held. To be owned by a Universal God that he experienced as inside his being in contrast to a God who is only outside. Form was integrating for him now. He prayed to the Father. “Father, empower me to follow. Make me a disciple.”

He got back in the car and travelled down the road until he came to a mountain stream. He stopped his car there beside the road. He exited the car and walked down the sloping embankment. He traversed the sturdy barbed wire fence. He came to the cold stream on his knees. He splashed the cold water on his face. “This place in the stream where I’ve come to is just deep enough to be immersed in.” the man thought to himself the unthinkable.

It was forty degrees outside. An occasional vehicle passed on the highway as the man sat by the stream considering the possibility of this next baptism. He was creating ceremonies for himself over and over again now. He was in the process of saying yes to another ceremony that was rooted in tradition but which contained the novelty of the expression of his Universal, but individual being in this moment.

The man considered the baptism but he dismissed it. He climbed the barbed wire fence, made his way back up the small embankment, got back in his car, started the engine and drove down the road. And in his willingness to walk away from an idea that was possibly inert or inane (possibly even ascetic in nature), he found another willingness. He became curious about the stream. He became curious about that space in the stream that was just deep enough to immerse a human body. He pulled his car over on the side of the road. He began to plan the logisitics of it. How he would get in the stream with only his underwear, while still wearing his clothes down there to climb the barbed wire fence. It was simple enough, but the practicalities seemed very important and he sat there for some time thinking about it until finally he knew that he wanted to do it. He did not feel that he was being ordered to do it. But he wanted to pray a prayer. He wanted to somehow make this body an offering. He wanted to say yes in a significant way to this discipleship. “Father, empower me to follow. Empower me to be a disciple.” These words would rarely stop flowing from the man’s mouth during this whole process, “Father, empower me to follow. Empower me to be a disciple,” he chanted as he walked himself through the baptism process, the ceremony that was being born in his heart.

The man turned the car around and returned to the same spot in the stream that he had driven away from just minutes ago. He descended the slope. He climbed the barbed wire. He stood for a moment, hoping that a car would not pass. He committed himself to this prayer. He committed himself to this ceremony that was being born of his own Being. He committed himself to this ceremony which was born so long ago and that was now being integrated into this man’s life.

He kicked off his shoes (he had already removed his socks in preaparation). He took off his shirt. It fell by his feet. He took off his favorite pants (the ones that he would find on Christmas day which still lie ahead of him). He removed his glasses and placed them in a shoe. He was now wearing only a a pair of black underwear. 

He quickly stepped into the cold cold water and kneeled as the water, for a brief moment rushed over his head, a moment that still lives deeply now in the writer’s being as the story is retold (the effect of ceremony that is born from a heart that is willing to participate in meaningful ceremony and a living Spirit supporting the efforts)

He came out of the water quickly, still chanting “Father, make me a disciple. Empower me to follow. Empower me to follow. Empower me to follow.” As he reached for his clothing he heard a car approaching. “Ahhhh!” Thought the man. “No! No!” He quickly picked up his clothes and ran for the cover of the nearest tree. It was too late. The car was already upon him as he was running to the tree, soaked underwear and hair. 

He stopped. He dressed as quickly as possible, hoping that the car would not turn around to investigate. Hoping that the people in the car were not near as curious as he was that day! He put on his clothing and ran away. It was not until he had traveled fifty feet that he realized that he had somehow left his glasses by the tree. He returned to the area carefully, trying to avoid a great crushing of the powerful tool that allowed him to see well enough to drive. He stepped softly. There they were, his glasses. He placed them on his face. He returned to the barbed wire. He climbed the barbed wire. He climbed the gentle embankment. He got in the car. He turned the ignition. The car started. He turned the heater on high. He checked his rearview mirror. He merged the little blue toyota onto the two lane mountain highway. He continued his chanting, “Empower me to follow, Make me a disciple, empower me to follow.”

It was in this way that the man found himself, once again, travelling down the road, a passenger in the little blue Toyota.

The man stopped a little ways up the road. Undressed. He changed his soaking underwear in the shelter of the blue car. He dried his hair with a shirt. And he continued his journey.

This is when he came to a mountain. The writer is not now aware of the qualifications for a mound of rock and dirt to be called a mountain. And how tall this mound of rock and dirt actually was is not recorded in any literal history. But the mound of rock and dirt seemed large enough, and daunting enough to earn the title of “mountain” in the mans heart that day. The mountain towered over the man as he passed under it on the ribbon of a road beneath its majesty. 

The man stopped the car. He looked up at the mountain. And this is when it happened. This is when the dialogue began.

“Father?”

This is where the space appeared to the man to be charged with presence. This is when the Son knew that he was heard. The Son did not need to hear the Father in order to know that the father was there. The presence of the Father was in the Son. And this is when the man spoke to the Son with the voice of the Father. He and the Father were one now.

“Yes, Son?”answered the Father. And the two of them, who were now one, stood there, looking up at the mountain. The rocks. The vegetation. The ups and the downs of it. The barbed wire fence that attempted to separate the road from the mountain.

“Father? Can I climb that mountain?”

And again. The presence that came with the silence. The presence and confidence that came with Spirit. The presence and the confidence that the young man had left behind so many years ago as he had walked away from his form. The resentments had come so strongly as the abused young man was condemned to replaying the critical voice of his earthly father. That presence that he had known so briefly before he gave himself away to something else was restored unto him. Here was the joy of his salvation. Here was the dialogue. The dialogue that made life, in this moment, very much worth living.

The father replied.
“Yes son. You can try. Just take it one step at a time. Let’s do it together.”

The man and his father walked toward the mountain together. They climbed the barbed wire fence, the father giving practical advice sometimes, helping his son to avoid injury.

“Okay, Son. Watch this fence. Be careful. I don’t want you to get hurt.”

“Thank you, Father. I am so glad to be here with you today. I am so glad to be your son. I feel safe when I am with you, Father.”


“Yes, Son I am very glad to be here with you too. Now, let’s just take this one step at a time, and don’t forget to stop and rest when you need to.”

“Yes, Father. Thank you. I will not forget.”

“Now watch your step here, this rock looks a little loose.”

And so their dialogue continued in this way as they made their way up the mountain one step at a time.

“This mountain is much more difficult to climb than I imagined, Father.”

“Yes, son, this is no easy task. Do you need to rest?”

“Yes Father, let us sit together here on this ridge and rest.”

As the Father and Son sat down the Son discovered a great treasure. It was a rock in which was embedded the spiral fossil of some living being that had breathed here on this planet long ago, perhaps when all of this was covered in a great sea. The fossil appeared to the son as the great serpent, the one who spirals into the infinite multiverse. The son was much amazed.

“Oh wow, Father. This is really cool. I like it so much. It speaks to me so deeply. I love being with you Father. I sense your presence in this rock, in this fossil. I sense the presence of the Mother all around me too. I sense the Christ Being in all that I see.”

“Yes son. We are all here. Just like Jung talked about. The ancient archetypes made manifest in the human consciousness and witnessed in our own consciousness.”

“Yes, Father. I like it when you speak like that. You voice fills me with deep love and respect for this mountain.”

“Son?”

The son left a space in order to feel the father’s presence. The man waited for the voice of the Father to arise from within his being. It did.”

“Yes, Father.”

More space arose from the eternal Being that is present in all of creation.

“My son, look out into this valley before you.” They were now half way up the mountain. “Do you see how everything is?”

The son looked out upon the valley from this vantage point. He breathed in the presence of all that he could see. The ribbon of road below him. The curving nature of the land forms. The scrub brush and the the stream by the road in which he’d been baptized. It was all there, just as it was. It needed to be nothing more for the son in that moment. He saw it, and it was good. “This all appears to be static. It appears now to you to be still. But all of this is not near as solid as it appears to you. Everything. As we embrace this seemingly invisible change, as we embrace the death of each moment and the birth of the new moment, we put an end to needless suffering in our beings, and then we begin to teach the world to do the same. We are all teaching, Son. This is the meaning of the Cosmic Christ. The Universal Christ. The one who understood to fall in the ground and die, to be born again to the next moment.”

“You’re mother will teach you more about how to be held by the earth. She will show you in the coming days how to sink into the soil. She will show you how to wait. The Son sat in the presence of the Father. He sat in the presence of the fossil which showed him the kundalini serpent. Half way up the mountain, where the Father had revealed these secrets to the son, The father and the son erected a monument made of stones. They placed the fossil stone on top of the altar.

“The Son did as he was directed and he found great joy as he felt himself carried up the mountain by the strength of the Universal Christ found in the feather.

And in this way the father and son continued their journey up the mountain that morning. They climbed. They rested. The father helped the son pace himself. The writer who now stood at the north facing mirror in the great kitchen paused. He drew another bath, knowing that he was not alone on this journey. He imagined the feather. He held it high over his head. He wondered if the feather still stood in the altar that he’d erected over three weeks ago on that unnamable pile of rocks and stone, that mountain.

Day 21
10:20AM

The middle-aged-man slipped into the warming waters of yet another bath. As he rested there in preparation for the last steps of this story, he recalled those backpacking treks up to higher-than-eleven-thousand-feet with his only son.

The first time they went, the son was only eleven years old. The middle-aged-man understood that it would be impossible for him to communicate to his son the challenges that lie ahead, for those challenges can only be understood once they are faced. However, the father attempted to alert his son to what it might feel like to be faced with ones own limitations as they ventured into the wildness of a mountain.

The middle-aged-man remembered that he had underestimated the immensity of a mountain once. He’d found himself lost with a group of people. Their descent was hampered by a ravine and a steep cliff. The ventured on and found themselves on a steep grade with crumbling rocks as the sun was quickly going down. They all made it down safely, but the man never forgot that experieince. He felt as if the group of day-hikers were being swallowed whole by and unforgiving entity. He was being taught a lesson that day by the wild-indigenous one.

And so it was with this wisdom in his heart that the man attempted to help his son to understand the seriousness of placing themselves in the wild. 

The mountain challenged the man’s eleven year old boy that day as they found themselves half way up the mountain. The son had lost his fishing pole and creel. The son was tired. He was overwhelmed by the enormity of the journey as he carried his pack on his back. The son collapsed in frustration in tears. The father watched. The father breathed. The father waited.

“Son,” said the father. “We are up on this mountain together. And there is no one to come and get us. Our phones do not work here. We must make a decision for ourselves. If your pack is too heavy and you cannot go on, we could leave your pack here and retreat down the mountain. Or, if you sit for a minute and breathe, we could carry on. We could pass the point of no return together. We could carry our packs up this incline, make our camp, start a fire, and eat some dinner together, having climbed this mountain.”

The son looked up at his father.

The son did not want to leave his pack and climb down the mountain.

The son knew the only path for him was up.

And so it came to pass that the father and the son continued their adventure that day, together. They made their camp. They arrived at their destination. They erected their shelter. They lit the fire. They cooked their meal. They slept close to one another in their two man tent, the father and his eleven year old son.

A song was born from their trips to the mountains:

“We were held by the mother of the mountain
As we made our way back down
With the root under foot
And the river down below
And the clouds making thunderin’ sounds”

And it was in this way that the writer found himself facing North, sitting in the great living room with the saltillo tile and the twenty foot vaulted ceiling in the home that he did not own. He sat in the home where he felt very comfortable in but had no capital investment. He sat there with meager financial prospects and a diminishing bank account. 

He sat there in the great living room facing North with great hope in his capacity to be found in this present moment. He sat at the end of the construction of this great scaffolding that he’d been constructing for the last twenty-one days. He sat there as Eli meowed and peeked out the window to his West. The middle-aged-man sat there without any obligation to listen to a voice which reinforced the great illusion of fear. He sat there with a great commitment to Love in his heart. With a great commitment to the death of this moment, and the resurrection of the next.

The middle-aged-man sat there in the great living room with you in his heart, dear reader. He sat there in the presence of all the ancestors who had come before him. He sat in the presence of the great singularity. In the presence of the great I AM. He sat in the presence of Lucy the austrolopithecus, an Eve of us all who’d risen up out of the heart of Africa. He sat in the presence of all that had arisen and become this consciousness that he was now experiencing. He sat in acknowledgement of the very presence of God which he now contacted in his own being. He sat in a moment that was greatly void of fear. The windchime chimed. A freight train whistled. Eli sat on the arm of the couch, peering out the window as the grey feral cat passed by. He sat in satisfaction of the form that he’d clung to for the last twenty one days. These words.

He prayed that we would all be directed back to the mother from which we arose. He prayed that we would answer the call of the great mother earth who wanted to integrate our suffering.
